articles.title_orig: Spain Calls Early Elections After Housing Crisis Roils Government: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Spain Calls Early Elections After Housing Crisis Roils Government: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
SÃ¡nchez's announcement comes after a series of measures to tackle the housing crisis was defeated in parliament on Friday
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.
The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.
In a televised address on Monday, SÃ¡nchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".
Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for SÃ¡nchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.
"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," SÃ¡nchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".
SÃ¡nchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.
Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.
Spanish prime minister calls snap election after housing protests
SÃ¡nchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority.
SÃ¡nchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide".
The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change".
The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid home led to public outcry
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September.
A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension.
She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital.
Protests over housing took place in Madrid on Saturday
Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home , but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing.
The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas.
The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".
The Spanish prime minister currently doesn't command a congressional majority
SÃ¡nchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months.
In April, his wife BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation.
She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by SÃ¡nchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition.
In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations.
And in June, SÃ¡nchez's former transport minister, JosÃ© Luis Ãbalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.

articles.title_orig: De Minaur reaches China Open final with Djokovic playing Medvedev next
articles.title_zh: De Minaur reaches China Open final with Djokovic playing Medvedev next
articles.content_orig:
Novak Djokovic has brushed aside ongoing injury-related struggles and produced a trademark comeback to defeat top seed Alexander Zverev 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 for a place in the China Open semifinals, extending his unbeaten record in the tournament.
Playing the ATP 500 event in Beijing for the first time since 2015, the six-time champion was pushed to the limit by reigning French Open and US Open champion Zverev, who delivered 19 aces in the match on Sunday.
Meeting for the first time in nearly 16 months, Djokovic struggled to contain the German’s power in the early stages as the 29-year-old Zverev claimed the opening set, but the Serb gradually worked his way into the match and refused to let his opponent pull away.
“I had a terrible start – two double faults at the beginning. It was quite cold, and honestly, I didn’t feel warmed up, but my fault,” Djokovic said.
“I gave him an early break, and then it was hard to come back in the first set.”
The contest was briefly interrupted by a moment of controversy when Zverev argued that the electronic advertising signage had gone dark during a rally and requested a video review after losing the point.
Replays showed a section of the signage had switched off although not as Zverev was missing the forehand. The chair umpire ordered the point to be replayed, prompting a frustrated exchange from Djokovic.
The turning point came late in the second set when Djokovic broke at 5-4 to level the match, shifting the momentum in his favour after a tightly contested battle.
With little separating the pair in the third, the Serbian struck again at 5-4 on the Zverev serve, securing the decisive break to seal the victory in two hours and 35 minutes.
“I was trying to be aggressive and come to the net and change up the pace, not giving the same pattern,” Djokovic said.
“I am just glad that I held my nerves, played good shots at important moments, 5-4 in the second and third.”
The pair had not met since Roland Garros in 2025, where Djokovic won in four sets, and Sunday’s encounter again highlighted the Serb’s ability to deliver under pressure despite a season disrupted by physical issues.
With the victory, Djokovic moved a step closer to a seventh China Open title and an elusive first trophy of the year while denying Zverev another opportunity to strengthen his bid for the world number one ranking.
Djokovic will face Daniil Medvedev in the semifinals after the Russian defeated Francisco Cerundolo 7-6(4), 6-3 earlier.
World number one Elena Rybakina withdrew from this month’s Wuhan Open due to a foot injury, tournament organisers said on Sunday, a day after the Kazakh suffered a shock defeat in her opening match at the China Open.
Rybakina, who lost to world number 118 Alina Charaeva in Beijing, said she would take time away from competition to recover.
“I’m very sorry to the fans who were looking forward to seeing me play,” Rybakina said in a story posted on the tournament’s Instagram account.
“I’ll take some time to rest and recover. Thank you for your understanding and continued support.”
The 27-year-old has been managing a lingering lower leg and foot problem that also forced her to retire from her Cincinnati quarterfinal against Iga Swiatek in August.
Despite the setback, Rybakina recovered in time for the US Open, where she claimed her third Grand Slam title , rose to world number one and became the first player to qualify for the season-ending WTA Finals.
Rybakina is next expected to compete this month in the Ningbo Open in China, where she will try to defend her title.
The Wuhan Open is scheduled to take place from October 12 to 18.

articles.title_orig: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.title_zh: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.content_orig:
UCSF’s $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital is scheduled to open in 2030, but it wont’t fix the university’s staffing crisis, write Drs. Akshar Rambachan and Anand Habib.
Every day, we watch our patients and fellow physicians pay the price for a strained system we didn’t build and can’t fix alone.
We are doctors at UCSF. At UCSF’s flagship Parnassus Hospital, people sick enough to need a hospital room wait on gurneys in emergency-room hallways because there aren’t enough staffed hospital beds.
We see patients attached to IV antibiotics laying on beds outside ER bathrooms. Elderly patients with hip fractures and pain languish under bright lights and constant noise until, deprived of sleep, they develop delirium. Families are forced to discuss end-of-life wishes within earshot of strangers in the hallway.
These are the daily realities at what should be a world-class health-care system. It’s a patient-care crisis driven by a dysfunctional system that we, as doctors, had no hand in building — or get a say in changing.
For generations, doctors had the authority and independence to make structural staffing choices to deliver high-quality patient care. Physicians owned practices, allowing them to control their patient load and shape the staffing team.
That world is disappearing. Physicians increasingly work as employees of sprawling health systems in which decisions about staffing, workload, compensation and budgets are made further and further from the bedside.
Whatever the administrators are doing clearly isn’t working. UCSF’s emergency wait time is more than 20% higher than the national average .
When UCSF patients are finally seen, their average length of patient stay is 60% higher than the state average — which strongly correlates with negative patient outcomes .
The Parnassus ER has more than double the national average of patients who leave without seeing doctors.
As doctors, we write emails, join committees, conduct studies and share proposals shaped by our years of training, research and experience to address this crisis. Our reports, requests, complaints and proposals are treated as suggestions and all but ignored.
That is why we and physicians across the University of California system are organizing a union.
The mayor and allied organizations say a ballot measure to spend $120 million on housing would create a ‘slush fund,’ but its advocates deny the charge
The number of new cases decreased last year by 8%, but community members are worried as changes to federal safety nets such as Medicaid take effect
Team supporters are celebrating the second playoff berth in as many seasons, creating game-day atmospheres that mirroring ‘Ballhalla’
UCSF’s solution to the patient care crisis is the $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital, scheduled to open in 2030. Let us be clear — we support the new hospital. Parnassus needs more critical inpatient and emergency rooms, and our patients deserve modern facilities.
But fancy new buildings don’t treat patients — people do. The expansion can’t be a substitute for solving the real crisis: the decreased investment in frontline staffing, resulting in chronic shortages that make it impossible to provide patients with world-class care.
We are often told that capital spending and staffing come from different budgetary “pots.” The accounting may separate capital and operating expenses, but the underlying finances are interconnected. UC’s own debt policy makes that clear: Medical centers seeking external financing must demonstrate adequate operating income, cash on hand and the ability to cover their debt payments .
In other words, financing what UCSF builds for tomorrow depends on the operating performance of the health system today — which is to say, on the people doing the work.
You cannot grow a system by hollowing out the front-line workers who make it run. Commitments to adequate staffing, sustainable workloads, and retention of the people required to operate new hospitals should not be revisited every budget cycle, revocable with every change in leadership. They should be codified and fixed to maintain continuity and quality.
To deliver on our mission to do everything in our power to get the best outcomes for our patients, doctors need a say not only in how we provide care, but also in the conditions within which that care happens.
We need mechanisms to ensure sufficient staffing at all levels, guardrails on how technology is used in patient care, and safe worksites that support healthy outcomes for our patients — not wait times that cause suffering and worsen their symptoms.
Through the UC Physicians Committee, doctors across specialties and campuses are organizing with University Professional and Technical Employees union, alongside many of the pharmacists, therapists and other professionals we already work with every day.
Together, we can codify common-sense policies so that every part of a patient’s care team is set up for success.
The Helen Diller Hospital is a promise about what UCSF intends to be in 2030. The medical professionals caring for San Franciscans today deserve a binding voice in what it is now. A union is how we get one, so that the institution we’re proud to work for can be the one that its patients were promised.
Dr. Akshar Rambachan is a hospital-medicine physician at UCSF. Dr. Anand Habib is an internal-medicine physician at UCSF.

articles.title_orig: China “tests layered approach to countering drone swarms”
articles.title_zh: China “tests layered approach to countering drone swarms”
articles.content_orig:
China’s state television CCTV News shared video footage on Sunday of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) counter-uncrewed aerial systems (C-UAS) units in training with laser weapons, integrated missile-gun systems and high-power microwave technology as a layered defence against hostile drones.
PLA troops conducted live-fire tactical drills involving multiple day and night scenarios, CCTV said, adding that radar was used to detect a “dense swarm of drones” at low altitude. The C-UAS units then used a combination of laser ‘dazzling’ and electromagnetic measures to disrupt the formation of the swarm. Interceptor drones were also deployed as well as anti-aircraft guns.
He Qing, a PLA serviceman quoted by CCTV, said the drills combined responses to different aerial threats with battlefield operations and the handling of unexpected situations in an unfamiliar, complex desert environment.
Image: A screenshot from CCTV via Global Times
The September issue of the 2026 Unmanned Airspace Global Counter-UAS Systems Directory is now available. The guide is the world’s only comprehensive, continually updated directory of global C-UAS companies and systems. It itemises over 1,000 C-UAS products and services with performance details, company sales and partnerships arrangements. It is updated every month and broken down into niche sub-sectors (net-capture, missiles, intercept drones, detectors etc) to give C-UAS procurement and industry personnel a unique perspective of global C-UAS technical capabilities and market positions. It is available in word, PDF and excel formats and Unmanned Airspace readers are eligible for a range of discounts. For more information about the Directory please contact the editor Philip Butterworth-Hayes at philip@unmannedairspace.info.

articles.title_orig: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.title_zh: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.content_orig:
Wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse and its numbers dwindled across New Zealand due to predators and habitat loss
The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “recovering” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild.
“The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme.
“Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.”
A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm.
It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland.
But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland.
Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said.
Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.
Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally recovering”.
“It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said.
New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests.
Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success.
By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes.
“That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.”

articles.title_orig: CIP, Grok Ventures Back One of the World’s Largest-Ever Battery Storage Systems in U.S.
articles.title_zh: CIP, Grok Ventures Back One of the World’s Largest-Ever Battery Storage Systems in U.S.
articles.content_orig:
Energy Transition / Private Equity & Venture Capital / Sustainable Finance
Kenny Fisher October 5, 2026
Industrial heat and power solution provider Antora Energy announced plans for a new Kansas- based 5.8 GWh thermal battery storage project, anticipated to become one of the largest battery storage systems in the world once completed, with backing from investors including Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners and Grok Ventures.
The new battery storage project will be based at renewable fuel producer Pratt Energy’s biorefinery in Pratt, Kansas. Alongside the new project announcement, Antora also announced an offtake agreement to supply around-the-clock energy to Pratt Energy.
Founded in 2018, California-based Antora develops thermal batteries that store low-cost electricity as heat in insulated blocks of solid carbon and deliver the stored energy around the clock as industrial heat or power.
The project’s third-party equity financing was led by Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) as part of its credit platform investments, and included participation from Australian climate-focused investment firm Grok Ventures and University Pension Plan Ontario (UPP).
Reiner Boehning, Partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, said:
“Antora has demonstrated something rare: sound technology, compelling economic fundamentals, and a clear path to repeatable deployment at scale. That gave us the conviction to partner with Antora on this project.”
Under the new offtake agreement, Antora will supply energy from the 5.8 GWh thermal battery system to Pratt Energy beginning in 2027. The battery will store low-cost electricity as heat in solid carbon blocks and supply that heat continuously to the biorefinery. The companies said that the project will improve Pratt’s operational efficiency and product competiveness, as well as supporting the company’s efforts toward producing 100% zero-carbon-intensity (CI) ethanol.
David Bierman, co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer of Antora, said:
“Our partnership with Pratt Energy delivers it, helping meet Kansas’s rising energy demand without increasing power bills for homes or businesses. This biorefinery project is creating jobs and spurring local investment without straining the resources the community depends on.”

articles.title_orig: Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
articles.title_zh: Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
articles.content_orig:
Far-right challenger and son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro put in a stronger than expected showing, with Lula calling the result ‘unexpected’
Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.
With 99.9% of votes counted, the 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president, Jair Bolsonaro, had won 47%, meaning he will now face a 25 October showdown with his 80-year-old rival. Lula received 45.1%. Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m.
Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite and is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, who included Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%.
Brazil’s far-right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, was elected to the lower house of congress. Bolsonaro’s former infrastructure minister, Tarcísio de Freitas, was reelected as governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s most populous and economically important state.
Of the 54 senators elected, 34 were from the right or far right.
Flávio Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital, Brasília, that the result signalled “the end of an era” for Lula’s Workers’ party. “Lula has fought seven presidential elections. He’s worried about power. I am worried about the future of Brazil,” he said.
​Speaking in Sāo Paulo, Lula put a brave face on a difficult night for the left. “We have just had a lesson in Brazilian democracy,” he said. “The result is often unexpected. We can never get everything we wanted. I confess to you that I was convinced I was going to win the election in the first round … But we have a second round.” Lula said Bolsonaro’s “dark past” would become clearer to voters in the lead-up to that vote. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil.”
Earlier, as he cast this vote, Lula said Latin America’s largest democracy faced a stark choice, highlighting his adversary’s well-documented links to members of Rio’s underworld , including once employing close relatives of a notorious contract killer.
Lula, who became Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and was returned to office in 2006 and 2022, is hoping to secure a historic fourth non-consecutive term in this year’s election.
Allies of the veteran leftwinger called the election a crucial battle in the fight against a far-right movement that less than four years ago brought chaos to the capital, Brasília, during an unsuccessful attempt to overturn the result of the 2022 election, when Lula beat the incumbent president, Jair Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro hopes winning the presidency will allow him to free his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after refusing to accept he had lost the last election to Lula. Ahead of the election he also called for tactical voting from conservatives who are not supporters of Bolsonarismo , but want to vote Lula out of power.
As well as the president, Brazil’s nearly 159 million voters were choosing state parliamentarians, 27 state governors, 513 members of the lower house and 54 members of the 81-seat senate. Bolsonaro supporters made the senate race a priority because senators are the only lawmakers who can impeach supreme court justices – a demand among Bolsonaristas since the court jailed the former president for attempting a coup.
Hundreds of leftwingers had gathered at the heart of Laranjeiras, one of Rio’s most leftwing neighbourhoods, hoping to celebrate a Lula win to the sound of samba. But the mood soured and tears were shed as the hours passed and Bolsonaro’s lead over Lula held.
“It’s so sad that the Brazilian people … have opted for so much retrogression,” said Marcelo Mac, one of the owners of Miolo, a leftwing bar in Laranjeiras, as the scale of the rightwing advance was confirmed on Sunday night.
Mac, 46, voiced perplexity that the son of the man who tried to stage a coup only four years ago was now in pole position to become Brazil’s next leader. “He’s such an abominable guy that he manages to be even worse than his father,” Mac said of Bolsonaro.
Beside the bar a yellow flag stamped with Lula’s face carried the slogan: “Turn left”. But Brazil had voted for a turn to the far right.
Bolsonaro seemed to have the wind in his sails in the final days before Sunday’s vote, amid public frustration at a cost of living crisis and urban violence.
But opinion polls failed to predict the scale of the rightwing triumph.
Shop assistant Italo Andrade dos Santos, ​a 31​-year-old Bolsonaro voter, had to keep his celebrations restrained behind the counter of the pharmacy where he was working a Sunday night shift. “I was a little disappointed because I expected Flávio to win in the first round​. But I’m happy he’s ahead,” said Santos, adding that he voted “more to get Lula out than for Flávio himself”.
Donald Trump became a key election issue , with Lula accusing the US president of trying to swing the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour in order to “colonise” Brazil and appropriate its natural resources. Bolsonaro has vowed to build a closer relationship with Trump, who hopes a rightwing victory will help him further cement US control over Latin America after the election of pro-Trump leaders in a succession of countries, including Chile, Colombia and Peru.

articles.title_orig: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
articles.title_zh: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
articles.content_orig:
By supplying Akash missile systems, New Delhi offers Central Asian nations a cheap, reliable alternative
Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the latest sales on Thursday last week, hinting at interest from elsewhere as he called the Akash “one of our success stories”.
Developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Akash is a home-grown, short-range surface-to-air missile system that can hit multiple targets at once and includes built-in protection against electronic jamming.
It can hit aerial targets between 100 metres and 20km (328 feet to 12½ miles) high, with an operational range of 4.5km to 25km, according to the Defence Ministry. Each 5.87-metre (19-foot) long missile weighs roughly 710kg (1,565lbs) and use command guidance to lock onto targets.

articles.title_orig: Trump Can Win Brazil and Still Lose It to China
articles.title_zh: Trump Can Win Brazil and Still Lose It to China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s Washington may be about to get the Brazil it wants, a major piece of the hemispheric puzzle falling into place for the so-called “Donroe Doctrine. "
Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, took 47 percent of the valid vote on Sunday to left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45 percent, setting up an October 25 runoff .
Trump has not formally endorsed him , but a Bolsonaro win would give the U.S. its friendliest government in Brasília since the elder Bolsonaro’s, just as Washington tries to loosen China’s grip on strategic supply chains.
China will look on nervously, but much of its groundwork in Brazil is already laid. Those foundations will be tough to break, even with a Trump-friendly Bolsonaro government in power.
The trade data shows why. In the first eight months of this year, Brazil exported $77.1 billion in goods to China, up 15 percent year-on-year, compared to just $24.1 billion to the U.S. , down 9.7 percent. That is a ratio of more than 3-to-1.
Two-way trade with China reached $128.6 billion, against $51.4 billion with the U.S. Brazil’s soybean sales to China alone outstripped everything it sold to America. And the gap is widening. A year earlier, the ratio was 2.5-to-1.
Brazil is physically closer to the U.S. and sits in the hemisphere over which Trump is asserting American hegemony. But Brasília is, in many ways, closer to Beijing than Washington.
To be sure, a Bolsonaro victory would be a real prize for Trump. But political alignment cannot repeal economic geography.
A new president can reset Brazil’s diplomatic posture in January. He cannot, at the wave of a hand, reroute the 305 million metric tons of cargo Brazil shipped to China in those eight months.
Trade on that scale doesn’t make Brazil China’s ally, though they are partnered through the BRICS bloc. But it means Beijing’s leverage depends less on who governs Brasília than on the material reality of who buys Brazil’s harvests and processes its minerals.
For evidence, look at Bolsonaro’s coalition. Brazil’s congressional farm caucus endorsed him days before the vote, and Mato Grosso, the heart of soy country, gave him about 65 percent .
Roughly 70 percent of Brazil’s soybean exports from January through August went to China. Washington cannot replace the Chinese customer. It competes with Brazil for it.
Trump’s 2025 deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping commits Beijing to buy at least 25 million metric tons of American soybeans a year through 2028. And since July, Washington has imposed a 25 percent tariff on most Brazilian goods .
Brazil has run this experiment before. Ahead of his 2018 election, Jair Bolsonaro visited Taiwan and accused China of buying Brazil . By October 2019, he was in Beijing , courting Chinese investment.
Over his term, trade with China grew, his government resisted U.S. pressure to shut Huawei out of Brazil’s 5G network entirely, and Brazil stayed in BRICS.
Rare earths, command of which will decide the great power competition in the 21 st century, make matters worse.
The younger Bolsonaro told CPAC in Texas in March that Brazil would be “the battleground where the future of the hemisphere will be fought,” and said he discussed rare earths with Trump in the Oval Office in May.
Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves but produced less than 1 percent of global output last year. The chokepoint isn’t the mine, but the refinery.
And here’s the difficult truth: China and Chinese-controlled firms handled 91 percent of the world’s rare-earth processing in 2024.
Pela Ema, a mine in the state of Goiás, is Washington’s showcase. About $5 billion in U.S.-backed loans, acquisition money, and price guarantees is converging on it, and last month a U.S. company bought its owner , Serra Verde.
Yet the mine yields only a mixed carbonate, an intermediate product. Separating its heavy rare earths requires a route the U.S. has not proved at commercial scale, so some output may be stockpiled.
Meanwhile, the company’s legacy contracts with Chinese processors run until the end of this year.
All of it unfolded on Lula’s watch, not a Bolsonaro. Washington’s push for Pela Ema was built on capital and guaranteed prices. No presidential sympathy needed.
What Washington still lacks is processing. No Brazilian president can conjure that. The reality is that America will rely on China for rare earths well into the 2030s .
Trump’s own January proclamation warned that even domestic mining does not safeguard national security if the U.S. “remains dependent on a foreign country for the processing.”
Washington’s has time, and it can move quickly. It assembled most of the Pela Ema package within months, and substantial new heavy-rare-earth separation capacity outside China is a few years away , roughly one Brazilian presidential term.
A Bolsonaro government could fast-track permits, court U.S. capital for new deposits, and deliver what Fernanda Magnotta of the Inter-American Dialogue expects: “ greater screening of investments in sensitive sectors .”
Pair that with U.S. tariff relief, and by 2030 Brazil could anchor a Western rare-earth supply chain even as its soybeans keep sailing to China.
The runoff can change the U.S.-China contest in Brazil without settling it. What happens next will take shape by the end of a Bolsonaro term, assuming, as all indications suggest, he will triumph in the next round.
If China’s share of Brazil’s exports, about 31 percent so far this year , has fallen below a quarter, Pela Ema’s heavy rare earths are being separated outside China at scale, and Chinese capital is screened out of strategic assets, then Washington won Brazil outright.
But if not, Trump won the palace and lost the ports.

articles.title_orig: FBI Arrests Alleged Chinese Agent Accused of Spying on Son of Taiwan Leader
articles.title_zh: FBI Arrests Alleged Chinese Agent Accused of Spying on Son of Taiwan Leader
articles.content_orig:
The FBI has arrested a “Chinese foreign agent” at Los Angeles International Airport accused of spying on the Taiwanese president’s son.
Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, was arrested on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, Bill Essayli, said in a post on X.
Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Zhang surveilled Taiwanese President William Lai Ching-te’s son, the FBI said. The agency did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a news article identifying him as Lai Ting-yu.
The US Justice Department said Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the behest of Chinese officials. She sent photos, video and license plate information of the Taiwanese leader’s son and his family to China.
Essayli called Zhang a “Chinese foreign agent” and said she “used tradecraft to avoid detection”.
“She never notified the Attorney General she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense,” he added.
Essayli said Zhang will appear in a Los Angeles federal court on Monday.
William Lai Ching-te and his Democratic Progressive Party say that Taiwan is already an independent country separate from China. Beijing views the island as Chinese territory.
Washington does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is bound by law to provide the island with the means to ‌defend itself.
Earlier this week, the US delivered two F-16V ⁠Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by China .
In January, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to achieve the “reunification” of China and Taiwan, calling Beijing’s long-held goal “unstoppable”.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI’s Altman: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology’
articles.title_zh: OpenAI’s Altman: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology’
articles.content_orig:
➡️ If you would like to receive this information in your inbox every morning before the markets open in New York, sign up here .
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico that people should accept the risks of AI in order to gain its benefits. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” he told the site. The trade-off will be worth it, he argued: “I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen’ … Because I think people will do tremendously—orders of magnitude more—good stuff than bad stuff.”
That’s a tone shift from Altman. When he talked to Fortune’s Alyson Shontell recently , he was more cautious. A 10% risk of AI killing us all by the end of the decade is unacceptable, Altman said. He insisted that OpenAI has not, and would not, take that risk.
“We are entering a new era,” he said. “We are clearly, today, at a point on the curve with great potential and real risk.”
“We have not solved alignment,” he said, referring to efforts to create AI that’s aligned with human values. “I believe no lab has solved alignment. I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong.”

The White House is monitoring a “plague” outbreak from a lab in Russia's Irkutsk region, according to CNBC . The incident began on Sept. 25 when a worker at an anti-plague research institute in eastern Siberia broke a test tube containing a “pneumonic plague pathogen,” according to Axios . She developed symptoms of pneumonia and then died in hospital during the night of Oct. 1-Oct. 2.
Local authorities then imposed quarantines and placed 189 people under medical observation. No further cases have been reported.
The global fertility rate for humans has never been lower, according to a recent deep-dive into global demographics from Moody's Ratings.
“The global fertility rate has declined from 4.9 children per woman in 1950 to around 2.2 today, only slightly above the replacement rate of 2.1,” the team there said. “More than 70% of the world's population now lives in countries with fertility rates at or below replacement level.” In Singapore, the government takes the problem so seriously it has started its own dating service for public employees .
The problem is that birth-rate shrinkage is a compounding problem, Moody’s says: “A fertility rate of 1.0 produces a generation roughly half the size of the one before it. At 0.8, population decline compounds even more rapidly. These effects take decades to emerge but are difficult to reverse.”
Estimates of future fertility are constantly being revised downward, as this chart from AllianceBernstein shows, implying that the problem is getting worse, faster:
A shrinking population of workers has negative consequences for economic growth, taxes, asset growth, governments’ ability to finance their debt, and inflation, most economists would agree.
Except AB’s Inigo Fraser Jenkins. “It’s probably a controversial view, but we think that fewer babies is actually a good thing. It is too late to curtail a warming of the planet by two degrees, but declining birth rates have broader implications for reducing the wider human impact on the planet and ameliorating the ‘Anthropocene.’ We are also scathing of ethical arguments that more babies are a ‘good.’”
(He and his team promised to elaborate in a forthcoming note.)
Gold has largely disappointed investors this year. After rising to around $5,340 per troy ounce at the beginning of the year, it has since lost 21% of its value and sits at $4,197. Gold now seems to be inversely correlated with U.S. interest rates, according to HSBC’s James Steel. If bonds pay higher yields, then gold (which never pays a dividend) makes less sense.
“The financial markets appear to be anticipating more substantial rate hikes, which helps explain recent gold weakness,” he said in a note. “This has been a key factor in reversing gold’s mid-summer rally.”
“As expectations for Fed rate hikes grew, gold prices weakened.”
The U.S. delivered a historically weak jobs report on Friday, with the Bureau of Labor Statistics reporting only 29,000 new roles created in September—way below expectations—and the unemployment rate moving up one tenth of a point to 4.2%.
It’s more evidence that AI is nibbling away at the job market, according to Samuel Tombs and Oliver Allen of Pantheon Macroeconomics. Although AI is creating jobs in construction and specialty trades, those gains were offset by larger declines in sectors that are the heaviest adopters of AI, like accounting, advertising, admin, legal, travel arrangement, software, and consulting.
The amount of revenue needed by the AI sector through 2032 in order to sustain its spending, according to Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of the Columbia Business School. That’s more than spending on energy, construction, computers, defense, or the internet, the WSJ noted .

This summer, with torrential rain threatening her outdoor wedding, a bride did the one thing left on her checklist. She hired an Etsy witch to cast a spell for clear skies. She’s not the only one, according to Fortune’s Tatiana Sataua . Her bridesmaid, Brooke Bekoff, was one of roughly eight bridesmaids, and of those she said five or six had hired Etsy witches for needs of their own.
“I remember that being like, ‘Wait a minute, this is such an interesting opportunity,’” Bekoff said. “There’s really something here culturally.” After the wedding, she built Divina, a marketplace where practitioners offer tarot readings, spell work, Reiki, astrology, and other spiritual services.
The U.S. psychic-services industry generated $2.3 billion in revenue in 2025, according to a July 2025 IBISWorld report, growing at an annualized rate of 5.5%.
As for the bride? The rain continued as she got ready. But then, in a moment Bekoff described as straight out of a movie, the clouds parted right as the bridal party headed outside. Sunlight replaced the downpour, and not a single drop fell during the ceremony until it started to pour again after it ended.

articles.title_orig: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
articles.title_zh: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
articles.content_orig:
China is accelerating its consolidation of smaller, mostly rural banks in a bid to shore up its financial system, amid ongoing concerns over an economic slowdown in the country.
Beijing's policy-led consolidation saw a record 670 lenders closed in 2025 — about one-quarter of banks in the country — as authorities ramped up mergers and dissolutions to create fewer, larger and better-capitalized institutions, according to Fitch Ratings analysis.
Small and rural commercial banks "remain the weakest part of the system" in China, Fitch said in a report , which flagged their "poor asset quality, low capitalization and governance shortcomings," especially in less-developed regions of the country.
The rating agency said the return on assets among rural banks fell to 0.45% in the first half, down from 0.56% in 2021. Meanwhile, non-performing loans among such lenders rose to 2.8% in the same period, ahead of the sector average of 1.5%, with greater exposure to smaller companies, property developers and local government funding vehicles.
The consolidation push is aimed at boosting oversight, curbing regulatory arbitrage and improving transparency, Fitch said, noting that stress at smaller lenders is unlikely to lead to system-wide contagion, pointing to their largely localized operations and limited interbank exposure.
The measures could "ultimately reshape competitive dynamics among smaller lenders, although their structural weaknesses may persist in the near term," the rating agency added.
The move comes amid ongoing signs of strain in the world's second-largest economy.
China's GDP grew 4.3% in the second quarter, its slowest pace since 2022 , while industrial profits came in at 4.2% annually in August, their weakest pace this year.

articles.title_orig: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.title_zh: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

articles.title_orig: WCC programme director strengthens strategic vision for ecumenical formation
articles.title_zh: WCC programme director strengthens strategic vision for ecumenical formation
articles.content_orig:
World Council of Churches (WCC) Programme Director for Unity, Mission and Ecumenical Formation Rev. Dr Kuzipa Nalwamba shared an update to the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation (EEF) meeting at the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey 4–9 October. Nalwamba emphasized that formation should be understood not simply as a collection of educational activities, but as a fundamental “ethos” of the WCC.
“The WCC is strengthening its strategic approach to Ecumenical Formation, positioning it as a central dimension of the organization’s life and work under its 2023–2030 Strategic Plan”, said Nalwamba.
Described as a “super transversal”, WCC’s Ecumenical Formation vision is being developed as connective tissue across the WCC’s thematic priorities and in relationship with member churches and ecumenical partners. It also seeks to interpret the WCC’s Journey of Justice, Reconciliation and Unity in educational and faith-nurture terms, ensuring that learning is both spiritually grounded and transformative.
The strategic approach includes a coherent programme of Ecumenism 101, Global and Regional Ecumenical Theological Institutes (GETIs/RETIs), and Bossey. The aim is to offer participants a connected learning journey rather than a series of separate activities.
The report also highlights sustainability through investment in pedagogy and the development of GETIs and RETIs as self-sustaining hubs capable of nurturing ecumenical leadership for future generations.
“If we do not equip the current and next generation with the tools to think ecumenically, the movement becomes unsustainable”, she said.
The EEF Commission has been invited to help shape how formation can continue to animate every aspect of the WCC’s journey towards unity.
The Commission will also participate in the celebration of the 80th anniversary of the institute on 7 October.

articles.title_zh: Live: Spanish Prime Minister Sánchez calls early election for November 29 after housing decrees rejected
articles.content_orig:
Spanish PM Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election days after Congress voted against measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis
SÃ¡nchez's government had presented the measures in response to nationwide protests, triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home for failing to pay a sharp rent increase
The woman's rent was raised from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension
SÃ¡nchez has been prime minister since 2018. Spain was not due to hold a general election until summer 2027 - here's what happened last time
Most polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election, which will take place on 29 November
SÃ¡nchez clearly wants to take the initiative - but it's going to be very tough for him to remain in power, writes Guy Hedgecoe in Madrid
Edited by Rorey Bosotti and Imogen James
Dan Woodland Live reporter
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election on 29 November, bringing forward the vote which was originally scheduled for the summer of 2027.
The move follows weeks of protests across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants, sparked last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home in Madrid following a sharp rent increase.
SÃ¡nchezâs leftist coalition government failed to pass emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis on Friday - but is now expected to approve measures on Tuesday.
The premier's position has also been marred by multiple corruption investigations in recent months involving former members of government and even his wife and brother.
Opposition parties welcomed the snap election, with the leader of the conservative People's Party Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o declaring Spain will "at last" say "what it thinks", and leader of the far-right Spanish party Vox Santiago Abascal saying he was "glad" about the announcement.
Meanwhile, members of SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians expressed confidence that they would be re-elected and the prime minister would "pull off a comeback".
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next vote, however they would be expected to need Vox's support to form a government.
This will be SÃ¡nchez's sixth election in 11 years, and if he is to remain in power, he needs to upset some tough odds, writes our reporter in Madrid .
We're ending our live coverage here, but you can read more in our news story .
With eight years in power, Pedro SÃ¡nchez is now Spain's second longest-serving prime minister in recent history.
His political career has been marked by dramatic twists and turns, including his resignation as Socialist Party leader in 2016 after losing the support of senior party figures. Just seven months later, he staged a remarkable comeback, returning to the leadership with the backing of grassroots members.
SÃ¡nchez has called an early election despite opinion polls suggesting he may struggle to secure enough support to remain in power.
Some analysts believe that focusing the campaign on Spain's housing crisis could help mobilise left-wing voters and steer the debate away from other challenges facing the government, including the situation in Ceuta and corruption allegations involving figures close to SÃ¡nchez.
It is not the first time SÃ¡nchez has taken a major political gamble. In 2023, he called a snap election after his party suffered heavy losses in regional and local elections.
Polls at the time also suggested he was heading for defeat.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, SÃ¡nchez ultimately secured enough parliamentary support to stay in office, thanks to agreements with left-wing parties and the backing of Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Opposition parties accused him of "selling out Spain" in order to remain in power.
The High Court of Justice of Madrid has rejected a request to disperse an encampment in Puerto Del Sol in the Spanish capital.
Protesters have set up tents in the famous square since 27 September, court documents show.
The court rejected the Community of Madrid's request for police to clear the square on Monday. A new hearing is expected to take place on Wednesday.
A trade union has also called on people to continue protesting in the street against issues with wages and housing ahead of the snap election.
The general secretary of the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) trade union confederation, Unai Sordo, says: "We must continue with a path of mobilisation, of street protests as we had announced, regarding wages and housing measures, and that will be our course in the coming months."
People in the streets of Madrid say they welcome news of the snap election called by Prime Minister SÃ¡nchez this morning.
âI think itâs good given the situation thatâs arisen", Raomon Diaz tells Reuters.
"Young people have been given little prospect for the future. And Iâd like to see a truly left-wing government finally come to power.â
Protester Florencio Diaz described the election announcement as a "great victory for the protests in the streets".
Florencio Diaz says Spanish people are struggling with the cost of living
"Weâre in a very difficult situation, with the cost of living rising and, above all, the abuse taking place in the housing market", he says.
However, Sandra - who is also protesting against Spain's housing crisis - expressed reservations about what the future holds.
âTo be honest, Iâm a bit worried about what might happen. But itâs certainly true that with the government we have, things arenât moving forward.â
Sandra says she's worried about Spain's future
The Spanish government is expected to approve measures on Tuesday aimed at tackling the housing crisis that parliament rejected last week .
The measures include a suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030 and an automatic renewal of rental contracts.
The government failed to pass them last week, after they were opposed by the People's Party (PP), Vox, and Junts.
Once the government approves the measures, SÃ¡nchez has 30 days to get them ratified. But the Madrid-based political newspaper Moncloa suggests that the prime minister's calling of a snap election could help him do this without congress, as parliament will be dissolved before those 30 days are up.
When congress isn't sitting, ratifying the measures falls to a committee which has a more favourable political make-up for SÃ¡nchez and doesn't require support from the Junts party, the newspaper says.
The deputy prime minister of Spain Yolanda DÃ­az has called for rent caps and a shortened workday
Members of Pedro SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians have continued to react to the Spanish snap election.
The deputy prime minister of Spain, Yolanda DÃ­az - who is part of the Sumar movement - says in a post on Bluesky: "We are going to win again."
DÃ­az says the group will cap rents, shorten the workday and raise the minimum wage.
Health minister MÃ³nica GarcÃ­a says in a post on X that the "Spanish people will rise to the occasion and prevail over the resentment of international hate".
Meanwhile Justice minister FÃ©lix BolaÃ±os says on X that the prime minister "will pull off a comeback" and leave the People's Party and Vox "without a government".
Catalan President Salvador Illa Roca says elections will be a "moment to decide between continuing to advance or going backwards". "Catalonia will stand with Pedro SÃ¡nchez," he adds.
SÃ¡nchez celebrates beside his wife Begona Gomez, after winning the general elections in 2019
These will be the sixth elections that Pedro SÃ¡nchez has contested as Socialist leader since 2015.
He has only won two of those - the 2019 ballot which was repeated after being inconclusive - and yet he has been in power since winning a no-confidence motion against his conservative predecessor, Mariano Rajoy, in 2018.

Manufactured by AVIC subsidiary the Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation, the Z-10 entered service with the PLA Army in late 2010. It began documented shipboard trials in 2014, when Chinese navy imagery showed a Z-10 landing on the Baxianshan Type 072A tank landing ship.
The attack helicopter’s maritime role has gradually expanded since then. In 2020, army helicopters practised landing, refuelling and rearming on a civilian semi-submersible.

articles.title_orig: Former Prince Andrew Files Legal Action Against U.K. Police After Arrest
articles.title_zh: Former Prince Andrew Files Legal Action Against U.K. Police After Arrest
articles.content_orig:
Former prince to challenge whether Thames Valley police acted lawfully over searches relating to his arrest
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking action against Thames Valley police to challenge the legality of search warrants that led to his arrest earlier this year, a judicial spokesperson has said.
A private high court hearing is due to take place before Mr Justice Hilliard on Thursday to determine whether documents related to the the former Duke of York’s call for a judicial review can be made public; with Thames Valley police in opposition.
The legal fight stems from the issuing of warrants by an Old Bailey judge that allowed police to raid Mountbatten-Windsor’s residence on the Sandringham estate, and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, in February. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files.
A high court judge subsequently granted him permission to challenge the legality of the force’s actions over the searches.
According to the Daily Telegraph, which first reported Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal challenge, it represented the first time a member of the royal family had challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on his 66th birthday in relation to allegations that when he was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.
Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with the late financier.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on 19 February and interviewed under caution before being released under investigation.
Misconduct in public office can cover a wide range of conduct, including sharing confidential financial information, financial misconduct, wilful neglect of duty and sexual misconduct. It also covers corruption and improper interference, conflict of interest, perverting the course of justice, dishonesty or fraudulent conduct, and misconduct leading to personal gain.
Thames Valley police said: “Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court. As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”
Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for comment.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump vs. Bernie Sanders—2 Sharply Different Views of America’s Role in the World
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump vs. Bernie Sanders—2 Sharply Different Views of America’s Role in the World
articles.content_orig:
One is an imperial gangster; the other seeks to create a world “not based on greed but based on justice, on decency.”
America’s century is over. History has not ended. This has become the new conventional wisdom even among the keepers of convention.
The challenge is how America finds real security in this new era. This month, we witnessed two strikingly different answers: one from the self-proclaimed most powerful man in the world, Donald Trump, and one from the champion of the rising populist movement on the left, Senator Bernie Sanders.
Trump’s address to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly was a characteristically grotesque performance, essentially a raised middle finger to the 190 country representatives gathered before him and the UN itself. Amid the routine farrago of lies, boasts, threats, and resentments, he presented a stark vision of America’s emerging role: essentially an imperial gangster—that, if pursued, constitutes a clear, present, and harrowing threat to this nation’s security.
After a stump speech preening about America’s primacy—“Our economy is the envy of the world. Our military is the most powerful on Earth. Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything. Our energy is fueling the planet”—Trump turned to America’s role in the world.
He boasted about the bombing of Iran, the “peace” in Gaza, the kidnapping of Venezuela’s president and control of its oil—“to the victor go the spoils”—the bombing of fishing boats in the Caribbean designated as “foreign terrorists,” the blockade of Cuba, “failing like never before and it will fail.”
Each of these—from aggressive acts of war to aiding and abetting genocide to illegal blockade—represent a brazen and open violation of international law and the UN Charter. Trump is saying that America will continue to police the world, only not to enforce the law but to enforce its will and to take what it can get. In apparent acknowledgment of the lawlessness, he issued a scurrilous attack on the International Criminal Court, “an evil group of people,” calling on all members to resign from the “rogue institution.”
Ironically, this fool’s errand of brazen plunder isn’t Trump’s greatest disservice to US national security. As the UN secretary general warned in his opening remarks, the world is struggling with the growing costs of real and present dangers that can no longer be ignored and can only be addressed by greater international cooperation: catastrophic climate change, global pandemics, corrosive inequality that undermines democracy and savages the poor, an accelerating nuclear arms race accompanied by the collapse of arms control agreements, and the known unknown of AI, which requires international regulation.
Trump made clear that the United States, under his watch, will sabotage any international regulation. Climate change and efforts to regulate AI are dismissed as a “hoax.” He has pulled the US out of the World Health Organization that monitors emerging pandemic threats and crippled our own Centers for Disease Control. Having pocketed billions while in office, he is the tribune of oligarchs, torpedoing all efforts at imposing a minimal tax on multinationals or on carbon or efforts to shut down tax-free zones. “There is no global government,” he preached, and “while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.” And, boasting about hiking America’s bloated military budget by one-third—to $1.5 trillion—and promising to build a “Global Dome” over America, he only adds fuel to the nuclear arms race.
At the dawn of the conservative era, Britain’s Margaret Thatcher asserted that “there was no alternative” to the neoliberal catechism. But there is an alternative course for the United States as it struggles to address new realities. It won’t come from a return to the failed “unipolar” globalism of the past decades. Instead, if there is an alternative to Trump’s gangsterism, it will come from the rising populist movement of the left.
Speaking on the eve of the UN General Assembly at Riverside Church in New York, Bernie Sanders offered a clear outline. He began with a tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King’s historic address at Riverside at the height of the Vietnam War, and his warning that “a nation that continues year after year to spend more money on military defense than on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death.”
He argued that not only is the US spending more and more on military weapons while turning its back on working people and the poor, but that “it is happening all over the world.”
To turn that around begins with a change in US policy, including “an end” to Trump’s “disastrous war on Iran,” termination of military aid to Israel and condemnation of “the genocide” in Gaza, work with grassroots activists to end “Putin’s disastrous war in Ukraine,” and denunciation of the UAE for aiding the genocide in Sudan’s civil war.
The growing violence, he argued, makes the United Nations more, not less, important, arguing that instead of arguing that “might makes right,” “our job is to strengthen the United Nations…and bring disagreements to the negotiating table…”
That would enable us to address the real and present security threats that we now face. At the top of that list, Sanders warns, is that “we are moving rapidly toward an extremely dangerous global oligarchy.” In nation after nation, we witness unprecedented levels of wealth and income inequality, illustrated by the fact that just as “the top 1 percent of America now owns more wealth than the bottom 94 percent,” the ratio is similar across the world.
“Children die of preventable diseases. People suffer every day. People give up hope. And 3,400 of the richest people on Earth became $4 trillion richer last year alone.”
The oligarchy, Sanders warned, “is ascending, working families are struggling to stay alive, and democracy is in retreat. The great challenge that we face in our country and all over the world is that that trend must be reversed.”
Sanders then turned to the other existential threats—focusing on the need to control the development of AI and to address catastrophic climate change.
The contrast is clear. For Trump, America strides the world. Our military will enforce our will. “The spoils” will go to the powerful, not to the people. Threats like AI and climate change are a “hoax.” International institutions are irrelevant if not evil.
For Sanders, militarism is a threat, not an answer. Basic security and democracy here and across the world are threatened primarily by an increasingly powerful and rapacious oligarchy. The emerging threats—climate change, AI (as well as pandemics and nuclear weapons, which he doesn’t mention)—require global cooperation. Changing our course depends not on building up the military but on building a progressive citizens movement here and across the world that can create a world “not based on greed but based on justice, on decency.”
Impossible? Perhaps, but Sanders reminds us of the “immortal words of Nelson Mandela: It always seems impossible until it is done.”
Katrina vanden Heuvel is editor and publisher of The Nation , America’s leading source of progressive politics and culture. An expert on international affairs and US politics, she is an award-winning columnist and frequent contributor to The Guardian . Vanden Heuvel is the author of several books, including The Change I Believe In: Fighting for Progress in the Age of Obama , and co-author (with Stephen F. Cohen) of Voices of Glasnost: Interviews with Gorbachev’s Reformers .

articles.title_orig: Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung shares overview of WCC education, formation
articles.title_zh: Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung shares overview of WCC education, formation
articles.content_orig:
Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung, moderator of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation, shared a report on 5 October that offered an overview of the commission ’ s most recent work as well as a glimpse of future plans.
A major development during 2025 was the Global Ecumenical Theological Institute (GETI) organised in connection with the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order under the theme “Where now for visible unity?” The programme included an online phase from 15 September to 12 October 2025 and a residential phase from 12–29 October 2025 in Wadi El Natrun, Egypt.
Chung described how GETI included theological lectures and facilitated group work, worship and community life, contextual and study visits, interreligious encounters, and direct interaction with the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order.
“ Ninety-five participants were admitted to GETI 2025, representing different regions and church traditions,” she said. “ A formal evaluation was undertaken following GETI. The results indicated a high level of overall satisfaction.”
Chung also described one of the major follow-up projects: the preparation of the publication GETI 2025: Voices and Visions of Transformative Unity, which will be launched 8 October. “ The publication records the theological work undertaken through GETI and serves as a resource for future ecumenical theological education and formation,” she said. “ Another significant area of work has been the development of Ecumenism 101, an introductory online course on ecumenism.”
The course has been developed as a means of making basic ecumenical knowledge and formation more widely accessible beyond residential programmes.
“ The course content is complete, with public release planned through the WCC website,” said Chung. “ Work on Regional Ecumenical Theological Institutes has continued as part of the effort to strengthen ecumenical formation in different regional contexts.”
During 2026, particular attention has been given to North America and Latin America.
“ In 2026, Bossey marks its 80th anniversary, having been established in 1946,” added Chung. “ The 2026–2027 academic year began in September 2026 with a new cohort of 33 students.”
She described how the institute continues to combine academic theological study with residential, intercultural. and inter-confessional community life. "Work has also continued to strengthen networks connected with ecumenical theological education,” continued Chung. “ The GETI 2025 evaluation demonstrated strong interest among participants in remaining connected after the programme.”
The 2026 WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation is meeting at the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey from 5–9 October. The Commission will also participate in the celebration of the 80th anniversary of the institute on 7 October.

articles.title_orig: Russia Cuts Coal Prices, Yet China and Türkiye Imports Keep Falling
articles.title_zh: Russia Cuts Coal Prices, Yet China and Türkiye Imports Keep Falling
articles.content_orig:
Russian coal exports to China fell 10.8% year over year in January-August 2026 as higher logistics costs, import duties, and stronger competition eroded Moscow’s position in one of its key markets.
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU) reported the figures on its official website on October 4. Russian suppliers delivered 53.15 million tons of coal to China during the eight-month period, losing ground to Mongolia and Indonesia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the agency, Mongolian coal imports surged 48.9% to 78.39 million tons, while Indonesia supplied 121 million tons. China imported 310 million tons of coal overall during the period.
Mongolia benefits from a shared land border with China and zero import duties, while Russian coal faces tariffs of 3% to 6%. Australia and Indonesia also receive zero-duty treatment under free-trade arrangements.
Russian producers are already offering discounts of around 10%, but further reductions could make exports unprofitable. Transport costs are adding further pressure, with the cost of shipping coal from Russia’s Vostochny port to China rising 45.5% from the start of 2026 through September 11.
Thermal coal exports could face the strongest pressure as Russian suppliers compete with Chinese mines while absorbing higher rail and freight costs. Russian railway tariffs increased again in October, while stronger demand for open freight wagons has raised transportation expenses.
The agency added that the pressure is also spreading beyond China. Russian coking coal exports to Türkiye fell 30% during the first seven months of 2026, with no shipments recorded in July, while coal deliveries to Russia’s southern ports dropped 33% that month compared with June.
The slump in southern deliveries coincides with mounting maritime risks in the Black Sea, where Ukrainian drone attacks on commercial vessels bound for Novorossiysk have driven up shipping costs.
Shipowners have pulled dozens of coal-transporting vessels from the region or halted operations altogether, and bulk carrier availability dropped by 21% in a single month. In early August, carriers serving the route raised freight rates by up to fourfold, while war-risk insurance premiums climbed to double or triple base freight rates.
