articles.title_orig: How Britain Learned to Love Chinese Cars—Especially a Look-Alike Range Rover
articles.title_zh: How Britain Learned to Love Chinese Cars—Especially a Look-Alike Range Rover
articles.content_orig:
My colleague José Pontes did a masterful report on the status of electric car sales in Europe last week. The news was all good, but I wanted to focus on one country where the news is particularly heartening for those who support the EV revolution. The bottom line is that in September, 2026, there were 99,199 electric cars sold in the UK — up a whopping 36 percent from September of last year — and more than double the rate of sales from three years ago.
British news service GBN reports sales of battery electric cars in the UK in September claimed a 28.3 percent market share, which is within striking distance of the 37.6 percent share attributable to gasoline powered cars.
The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders said new car sales were up more than 12 percent in September, the tenth month in a row that new car sales have increased. It attributed the increase in EV sales to an unprecedented number of model choices — especially in the smaller segments, compelling discounts, as well as the government’s electric car grant. The desire not to spend one’s entire paycheck to purchase gasoline was surely a factor as well.
Mike Hawes, the CEO of SMMT, said in a statement, “September’s record EV performance is a major achievement. Drivers are increasingly embracing the growing choice of models made available, and high fuel prices are also undoubtedly giving more consumers reason to consider going electric. The industry’s commitment is clear, with billions of pounds of investment in new models, new technology, and incentives.”
Here are the top ten best selling EV models in the UK in September:
Sales of hybrid cars were down 4.2 percent in September with a market share of 13 percent, but sales of plug-in hybrids surged by almost 56 percent to claim a 17 percent market share. In all, hybrids, EVs and PHEVs had a combined market share of 58.4 percent — an extraordinary number!
In the US , hybrids in September had a market share of around 18 percent, EVs around 7 percent, with PHEVs less than 2 percent. Stats like that prompted regular reader Are Hansen of Norway to ask recently if electric car sales in the US are the lowest of any country in the world. We don’t have current stats for all 195 nations , but it seems likely the US could well be at the bottom of the heap. Greatness means different things to different people, apparently.
SMMT said that since 2023 the number of BEV models on the market in the UK has more than doubled to 178. There are now 110 PHEV models and 50 hybrid models. In total, three quarters of all the new car models available in the UK are “electrified,” meaning they are either a hybrid, a plug-in hybrid, or an EV.
According to The Independent , 20 percent of new car sales in the UK in September were from Chinese brands such as BYD, Jaecoo, Chery, Omoda, Changan, or Geely. The Ford Puma is the best selling car in the UK this year, but the Jaecoo 7 — which looks a lot like the iconic Range Rover — is in second place overall. More than 10,000 of them were sold in the UK last month.
BYD, with 20,140 cars sold, is up more than 80 percent in the UK so far this year, putting it in second place in total sales behind Volkswagen. Kia is in third place, followed by MG and Audi. Tesla is in sixth place, just ahead of BMW. The Model 3 was the second best selling car in September, with the Model Y in fifth place.
“These figures are an incredible result for BYD, so I’d like to say a big thank you to all of our customers who buy our cars and enjoy them on a daily basis,” said Steve Beattie, deputy manager for BYD UK. “While it’s a huge result for us, we believe that there is still more to come. We’ve launched several other cars recently or are about to.
“The Dolphin G takes us into the hugely popular super-mini segment, and despite the car only arriving with our retailers in August, we’ve already taken over 500 orders. Pre-orders for the seven seat Ti 7 SUV are proving extremely strong, and the Shark pickup is generating a huge amount of interest too. I can’t wait to see what the rest of the year brings.”
Chinese brands also dominated the list of fastest growing brands, with Changan and Chery seeing strong growth, as is Leapmotor, which is partly owned by Stellantis and sells its cars at dealers that also carry Vauxhall, Citroen, Peugeot, and Fiat models.
Traditional brands are the biggest losers so far this year. Fiat sales are down more than 27 percent and Peugeot is down 16 percent. Seat, which is part of the Volkswagen Group, has seen its sale plummet by 28 percent, Mazda is down 17 percent, Honda is down 16 percent, and both Nissan and Hyundai have fallen by more than 16 percent so far this year.
Despite all the good news about EVs in the UK, that country has mandated they be 33 percent of sales next year. Mike Hawes of SMMT said, “Despite all these factors, uptake remains behind mandated targets and, whilst flexibilities help, the UK still has the world’s toughest targets and highest energy costs.” Calls to adjust that mandate are increasing as the end of 2026 gets closer.
A spokesperson for the Department of Transportation told The Independent, “September was another record breaking month for electric car sales in the UK — up 36 percent in a year and nearly 100,000 electric cars sold in a single month alone. The EV revolution is really picking up speed now, and it’s never been cheaper or easier to go electric.
“Our £2 billion Electric Car Grant is already helping over 190,000 drivers make the switch, backed by £600 million to roll out hundreds of thousands more chargers. While global fuel prices keep fluctuating, the message is clear — electric isn’t just the future, it’s the present, and we’re making sure Britain leads the charge.”

articles.title_orig: Season of Creation closes—but actions will continue
articles.title_zh: Season of Creation closes—but actions will continue
articles.content_orig:
As the Season of Creation officially closed on 4 October, people gathered online from across the world for a prayer service that not only recapped many green initiatives but also encouraged ongoing action to care for creation.
Speakers reflected on this year ’ s theme, "Living Water" (Ezekiel 47:9, 12): "Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live . . . Their fruit will be for food and their leaves for healing" (NRSV).
Analisa Ramsahai, environmental scientist and Catholic climate activist from Trinidad and Tobago, who serves as a board director and secretary for the global Laudato Si' Movement, focused on water as connection—our connection with each other, with the earth, and with God. “ Rain returns water to the earth, nourishing plants, animals and people,” she said. “ But before we explore these connections, I invite you to experience water for a moment.”
She then invited those gathered to imagine—and deeply appreciate—all the ways in which water touches their lives.
Elizabeth Trice, a UK-based wildlife and conservation professional and an active environmental organizer within the Church of England, and founder of “ The Seedlings Network,” expressed her appreciation for the gathering. “ It ’ s key to look back at our beginnings,” she said, referring to water being connected with the origins of all life.
“ It ’ s also important to remember that the voices of tomorrow are also the voices of today,” she added, noting that young people are not just carrying the future of the earth but also the present.
Fr Movses (Garen) Yosolkanian, Armenian Apostolic, with the Middle East Council of Churches (MECC), noted that water is a gift from God, a source of life, healing, and restoration. “ Yet we find ourselves in a thirsty moment in the struggle for global ecological justice,” he said. “ Across the world, our water sources are threatened. What should be a source of life is increasingly becoming a source of struggle, injustice, and division.”
Marí a Jos é Tejedor Gonz ález, with the ACT Alliance, thanked the speakers, those who began and continued earth-friendly initiatives, and all those who prayed. “ You all inspire us with your wisdom, hope, and witness throughout this season,” she said. “ You remind us that caring for creation is a shared calling. Although today marks the end of this year ’ s celebration, the journey continues.”
Season of Creation is the ecumenical world's month of prayer and action for creation. Beginning with “Feast of Creation in Christ” on 1 September, is a time of witness to God ’ s love and our human responsibility.
The season forms one chapter in the World Council of Church's Ecumenical Decade of Climate Justice Action (2025–2034), launched in Johannesburg in 2025.

articles.title_orig: Police investigating Flydubai co-pilot’s Australia ties
articles.title_zh: Police investigating Flydubai co-pilot’s Australia ties
articles.content_orig:
Authorities have said they are investigating the links of the co-pilot of the Israel-bound Flydubai flight with Australia.
A multi-agency Australian police and intelligence team – the Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team – is carrying out the probe, a spokesperson said on Sunday.
Mystery surrounds the co-pilot, who is accused of attacking the captain with an axe and attempting to seize control of Flight FZ1073 from Dubai as it approached Israel, and how he was able to acquire his seat in the plane’s cockpit.
He has been identified in media reports as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami .
He had been barred from flying in his own country because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views, The Associated Press news agency cited sources as saying.
While al-Hammami reportedly spent part of his life in the United Arab Emirates, the Reuters news agency, citing sources briefed on the Australian investigation, reported that he studied at a university in the Australian city of Melbourne.
A third unnamed source told the agency that he studied at RMIT University, a public research university in Melbourne, about a decade ago.
The Financial Times also reported al-Hammami’s links to Australia. Citing two sources familiar with the Australian investigation, the FT said al-Hammami had allegedly visited what it described as “radical mosques and extremist websites” while in the country.
Disaster was averted after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot and a reserve pilot took over its controls and completed an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
However, the case has raised questions about security in Israel, which has some of the world’s strictest aviation security measures.
The prosecutor general of the UAE, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, has labelled the attack an attempted “terrorist act”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there.
Netanyahu said a “loophole” appears to have allowed the Omani pilot to take part in the Flydubai flight, and that Israel would now strengthen its checks.
The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest “terrorist” attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over.

articles.title_orig: The mispricing of war
articles.title_zh: The mispricing of war
articles.content_orig:
The true price of war is rarely paid by those who start it. In a deeply interconnected world economy, the financial burden of conflict is increasingly exported through inflation, disrupted trade and slowing growth worldwide
In the space of just a few weeks, the throttling of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has revealed the true nature of the US-Israeli war with Iran. This is no regional conflict, because the entire world is being invoiced. While the size of the bill remains to be determined, it is already obvious that the belligerents won’t be the only ones paying the tab. War is typically framed in terms of national security, territorial integrity, humanitarianism, or even civilisational struggle. But such rationales obscure an unsettling truth: war is one of the most mispriced of human activities. Those who initiate it rarely bear the full costs, which tend to be displaced across borders, markets and time. Beyond the physical destruction, war generates massive negative externalities. The price paid by the perpetrator reflects only a small fraction of the social cost.
Of course, the intuition that war imposes downstream costs on others is deeply embedded in the political-economy literature, running from Adam Smith and David Ricardo to John Maynard Keynes and Karl Polanyi. But globalisation has transformed the effect into a structural feature of the modern economy.
Economic growth diminishing Consider the arithmetic of the current Iran conflict. Beyond the loss of life, direct US military spending may run into the tens or even hundreds of billions of dollars. Yet the broader economic cost – transmitted through energy, food and financial markets – runs far higher. The International Monetary Fund warns that the war is already diminishing many economies’ growth prospects, as energy shocks ripple outward and inflationary pressures intensify.
The transmission mechanism is brutally simple. When oil and gas prices rise, transportation and electricity become more expensive. When fertiliser costs increase, so do food prices. Central banks may respond by assuming a tighter monetary-policy stance. Ultimately, growth slows. Yet this domino effect is missing from the actual war ledger. Efforts to measure the true costs of war have consistently found that they lie beyond the battlefield. In their work on the Iraq war, Joseph Stiglitz and Linda Bilmes tallied a catalogue of costs in the trillions of dollars once macroeconomic effects were included. Similarly, both the IMF and the World Bank have found that violent conflict depresses growth in economies far removed from it.
Even under conservative assumptions, the US may bear only a modest share of the total global economic damage (much as the negative spillovers of the war in Ukraine far exceed the direct cost to Russia). As European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde recently cautioned, the rest is diffused across the system, absorbed by energy importers, emerging markets and households worldwide. War, in this sense, is globally subsidised.
Three mechanisms make this possible. The first is spatial. Modern economies are deeply interconnected. When war disrupts one node (particularly an energy chokepoint), the effects cascade outward. The Strait of Hormuz is not simply a geographic passage but a structural vulnerability in the global economy. The second mechanism is temporal. War typically requires the present to borrow from the future. Governments finance conflict through debt, deferring its cost to generations not yet politically represented. The fiscal consequences of past wars continue to unfold decades later, showing up in public debt, constrained policy options, and obligations that outlast the politics that created them.
The third mechanism is distributive. War concentrates decision-making while dispersing the costs. Those who decide are not the ones who pay. This last insight lies at the heart of modern conflict economics. The Oxford University economist Paul Collier has shown that wars persist not because they are collectively rational, but because they are privately beneficial. Small groups capture the gains as the broader population absorbs the losses. Today’s networked economy amplifies this asymmetry.
When the world pays the price As Edward Fishman of the Centre on Global Energy Policy argues in his book Chokepoints, power today flows through global systems such as energy routes, financial networks and supply chains. But conflict turns these into channels for economic contagion. The result is a peculiar inversion. War appears expensive in theory but affordable in practice, because much of the bill is paid by others. This mispricing has predictable consequences. When goods are subsidised, we get more of them. When their price is too low, we get oversupply: too much pollution, too much risk and too much war.
The policy challenge is therefore familiar, even if the politics are not: to discourage war, its costs must be internalised. Those who initiate conflict must bear a greater share (or, even better, the entirety) of its true costs. Ensuring that outcome requires an effective global institution that can align the private and social costs of conflict more effectively than global markets can. Until the world can come up with such an institution, the incentives will remain perverse, because one of the most destructive activities imaginable seems so affordable to those who undertake it.

articles.title_orig: How the Midterms Could Complicate the Supreme Court’s New Term
articles.title_zh: How the Midterms Could Complicate the Supreme Court’s New Term
articles.content_orig:
When the Supreme Court kicks off a new, nine-month term on Monday, one key player will be noticeably absent: President Donald Trump.
After months of near-constant confrontation with the White House, the nine justices will retake their seats behind the court’s mahogany bench without a docket full of Trump-driven, separation-of-powers blockbusters that defined the last term — from tariffs to birthright citizenship to the firing of once- independent government officials .
The respite is unlikely to last.
In the coming weeks, the justices will decide whether to wade into Trump’s messy defamation brawl with magazine columnist E. Jean Carroll , his mass cancellation of federal research grants , whether the Department of Government Efficiency must provide records detailing its slashing of federal agencies last year, and the administration’s ban on transgender Americans serving in the military.
Those and other cases could be added to a term that already includes an important Second Amendment challenge to bans on AR-15 rifles , the most significant case dealing with climate change to reach the justices in nearly two decades, and a fight over whether religious preschools receiving taxpayer money may decline to enroll the children of same-sex couples.
So far this next term, the court has granted 28 cases, less than half of what the justices will likely decide by June.
“There’s a very good chance that the 35 or so that the court is likely to grant in the remainder of the year will be the ones that are really the highlights,” Masha Hansford, an attorney at Davis Polk & Wardwell and a former assistant to the solicitor general, said at a recent event organized by the National Constitution Center.
One area where the court is already delving into Trump’s policies this term is immigration. The court has announced in recent days that it will hear arguments over the president’s mandatory detention policy and his push to deport migrants to countries other than their homeland. While important, neither of those cases has drawn the same level of attention as last year’s birthright citizenship case.
After Trump and his allies launched a rhetorical war against lower courts in early 2025, the president and the Supreme Court seemed to slide into a détente by the middle of the year — a delicate dance in which Trump has abided by the losses handed to him by the high court even as he has occasionally lashed out against the justices who supported them.
The court overwhelmingly sided with Trump on its emergency docket — the fast-track cases that are usually decided without argument. And it also backed the president in major regular cases that were argued during the last term and resulted in full opinions. One of those included the blockbuster decision allowing him to fire the leaders of agencies like the Federal Trade Commission . But the court was also willing to push back against Trump in some of those cases, such as by rejecting his emergency global tariffs and his push to undo birthright citizenship as it had been understood for more than a century.
Still, Trump has not shied away from railing against the 6-3 conservative court this past summer, including the three justices — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — whom he named to the bench during his first term. Trump told Time Magazine last week that he regretted nominated them.
“I gave them ​the position of a lifetime,” the president lamented, “and they vote against me often.”
The justices themselves have largely demurred when asked about Trump’s unusually personal attacks on the court. Justice Samuel Alito, a conservative who spoke to CBS as he prepares to publish a new book this week, said there has been a “great change in what presidents have said about the court when they are unhappy about our decisions.”
But, Alito said, that “very harsh” criticism has been “bipartisan.”
Pressed on Trump’s harsher statements, Alito said, “he has his own way of saying things.”
Before the court decides any of the regular — or merits — cases it has granted, there’s a chance it will have to deal with a flood of litigation tied to next month’s midterm election. Whether that is a deluge or a trickle may be in voters’ hands.
Derek Muller, a law professor and election law expert at Notre Dame, said he believes the likelihood of post-election litigation will be low “because there probably won’t be enough decisively close cases where litigation would really matter.” But, he said, “if it does happen, it could significantly transform the upcoming Supreme Court term.”
The court has already juggled a series of redistricting disputes spun off from the president’s push for a mid-decade redrawing of House district boundaries . And last month it shut down Trump’s controversial proposal to give the US Postal Service a role in screening — and potentially rejecting — mail ballots sent to voters across the country.
Also waiting in the wings are several important non-Trump merits cases that could define the 2026-2027 term. It seems almost inevitable that the court will review state laws requiring the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms. Moreover, a legal battle raging between prediction sites like Kalshi and Polymarket and state governments has already reached the high court and could make its way to an oral argument sometime next year.
The court’s conservative majority has been steadily expanding gun rights under the Second Amendment for years. It have a huge opportunity to do so again this term.
In December, the court will hear arguments in cases challenging bans on AR-15 rifles enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois. Gun rights groups say the semi-automatic rifles are widely owned by Americans and are permitted in the vast majority of states. Gun control advocates counter that the weapons have been frequently used in mass shootings and should not receive Second Amendment protection because they are more “dangerous” and “unusual” than other types of guns.
The case draws heavily on a landmark 2008 decision from the Supreme Court, District of Columbia v. Heller , which stood for the prospect that arms “in common use” are protected under the Second Amendment.
“I think we know how this case is going to come out,” Deepak Gupta, a veteran appellate attorney, said at a recent event hosted by the Georgetown Law Center, suggesting that the court would likely strike down the AR-15 bans. “We know the outcome, but we don’t know how it’s going to be decided.”
On the very first day of the term, the justices will confront a long-running dispute about whether cities and states may sue fossil fuel companies for billions of dollars in damages caused by climate change. The appeal before the court deals with one such suit from Boulder, Colorado, but the decision will almost certainly play into dozens of other pending cases filed by cities and states attempting to hold oil companies accountable.
ExxonMobil and Suncor, the two companies that brought the case to the high court, argue that climate pollution is inherently a federal issue, in part because emissions waft across state lines. That understanding of federal control, they say, should effectively supersede state law. But Boulder says that there’s nothing in the Constitution or in federal law that backs up ExxonMobil’s position, and that the Supreme Court should let the lawsuit proceed.
Particularly notable is Alito’s decision to recuse himself from the case because of stock he owns in fossil fuel companies such as ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. That opens the possibility of a 4-4 split, a rare outcome that would uphold the decision by Colorado’s Supreme Court that allowed Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed without setting a precedent.

articles.title_orig: Then and Now: World War I cenotaph
articles.title_zh: Then and Now: World War I cenotaph
articles.content_orig:
The 13th celebration of Armistice Day in Spokane is remembered for some monumental events.
Although it was a Tuesday, almost all businesses in downtown Spokane closed in honor of the day’s schedule. Most notable was the 12:30 p.m. unveiling of the 12-foot bronze statue of President Abraham Lincoln on a pedestal at Main Avenue and Monroe Street, surrounded by thousands who had just watched the Armistice Day parade. Among the attendees was one of the last Civil War veterans of the region.
But earlier that same day, Spokane’s American Legion Post 9 dedicated a solemn stone cenotaph at Riverside Cemetery, now called Riverside Memorial Park. The 19-by-26-foot platform, made from granite quarried in the Dishman area, consisted of a speaker’s rostrum surrounded by a wall lined with benches and an 8-foot arched stone with the inscription: “In Memory of Those Who Gave Their Lives for their Country in the World War.”
Legion member and architect Henry Bertelsen designed the monument and stonecutter Julian Mosfelt Simonson, also a member, carved the stone. As is typical with a cenotaph, meaning “empty tomb,” no names are inscribed there.
During the war from 1914-18, 11,000 Spokane men served in the military, more than 4,000 went to Europe and almost 200 men from Spokane died in the war.
Almost 500 people attended the dedication, where tearful Gold Star mothers took seats on the cold stone benches surrounding the platform while veterans and families gathered around.
The American Legion was founded in 1919 by the weary veterans of the war in Europe. From its inception, the Legion endeavored to honor past military service, including those from the Civil War and the Spanish -American War. The group would also advocate for veterans benefits and  comfort the bereaved.
Both built in 1920, the Argonne Road bridge and Marne Bridge over Latah Creek were dedicated to returning war veterans, but Legion members wanted to do more. The veterans sold poppies and held other fundraisers to raise the $7,500 to build the memorial, which would be situated near veterans’ burial areas so the platform could be used for future burials.
Some 20 years after the 1930 dedication, an “S” was added to the inscription, changing “World War” to “Wars.”

articles.title_orig: Asian stocks rise as weak U.S. jobs data eases Fed hike bets; Japan surges
articles.title_zh: Asian stocks rise as weak U.S. jobs data eases Fed hike bets; Japan surges
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Asian stocks rose broadly on Monday, with markets in mainland China and South Korea closed for holidays.
The focus shifted to the release of the Institute for Supply Management's services purchasing managers' index later in the day and the minutes of the September meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee on Wednesday.
Softer US jobs data reinforced expectations that the US Federal Reserve may hold interest rates steady later this month.
The US dollar was firm in Asian trade and bond yields steadied, while gold edged up slightly to hold above $4,150 an ounce, recovering from an early slide.
Brent crude futures fell nearly 1% towards $101 a barrel after gaining almost 5% last week.
Amid rising risks to global supplies, major OPEC+ members agreed over the weekend to leave production quotas unchanged next month.
Yemen's government forces said on Sunday that they had struck Houthi targets in the capital, Sanaa, and in Taiz in the south-west, deepening the conflict ravaging one of the world's poorest countries and the wider region.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index finished 0.28% higher at 24,040.34, as selling pressure on interest-rate-sensitive property and financial shares offset gains in technology stocks.
Japanese markets climbed sharply as investors bought chip-related stocks following a rise in US stocks on Friday.
The Nikkei average closed 2.4% higher at 69,946.86 after briefly crossing 70,000 for the first time in three months.
The broader Topix index advanced 1.33% to 4,145.22. Among the top gainers were SoftBank Group, a Japanese technology and investment group; Advantest, a Japanese semiconductor testing equipment maker; and Tokyo Electron, a Japanese semiconductor equipment maker. Their shares rose 3% to 6%. Shares in Japanese banking groups Mitsubishi UFJ Financial and Sumitomo Mitsui Financial rose around 2% each.
Investors shrugged off data showing that Japan's service sector expanded at a weaker pace in September. The Japanese yen was little changed ahead of a series of economic reports due this week.
Japan no longer needs expansionary fiscal and monetary policies aimed at boosting demand, former Bank of Japan board member Asahi Noguchi said in an interview on Friday. His remarks reinforced expectations that the central bank could raise interest rates again as early as December.
Australian markets gave up early gains to finish marginally higher, led by gains in healthcare stocks. Australian biopharmaceutical company CSL rose about 1% after agreeing to pay up to $1.6 billion to jointly develop and commercialize an experimental treatment for rare kidney and liver diseases.
Australian biotech company PYC Therapeutics rallied 3.7%, while Cochlear, an Australian hearing implant maker, surged 4.2%. Macmahon Holdings, an Australian mining services company, jumped 4.5% after securing a $98 million contract extension at the Daisy Milano Gold Mine.
Across the Tasman, New Zealand's benchmark S&P/NZX-50 index edged up 0.14% to 13,699.02, halting losses from the previous two sessions.
US stocks closed higher on Friday as data showing much weaker-than-expected job growth in September reduced expectations of a potential Federal Reserve rate hike later this month.
Data showed that non-farm payroll employment rose by 29,000 jobs in September, after an increase of a downwardly revised 133,000 jobs in August. Economists had expected employment to increase by 85,000 jobs.
Wage pressures were lower than expected. The unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% from 4.1% in August, while economists had expected it to remain unchanged. Separate data showed factory orders rose less than expected in August.
Bond yields rose as hawkish comments from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan offset the softer jobs data. Logan called for short-term borrowing costs to rise by at least another 50 basis points.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite surged 1.2% to a new record high, while the S&P 500 advanced 0.7% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.5%.

articles.title_orig: “Affirmation of Just Peace” published by international peace convocation in Korea
articles.title_zh: “Affirmation of Just Peace” published by international peace convocation in Korea
articles.content_orig:
An International Ecumenical Peace Convocation held, 9-13 September in South Korea, has released an “ Affirmation of Just Peace. ”
The convocation was convened by the National Council of Churches in Korea, Christian Conference of Asia, and World Council of Churches.
“ During our conference we listened to voices from Palestine where the violence of war and injustice continues unabated and from Ukraine where there is no end in sight to the war, ” reads the document. “ We heard voices from the Philippines where human rights violations continue, and concerning the oppression of ethnic minorities in Sri Lanka. ”
The text names other forms of armed conflict and structural and state violence that persist across the world. “ Political tensions are escalating and militarism is intensifying among countries aligned with opposing blocs, while the battlefield deployment of AI-enabled weapons systems and even the growing threat of nuclear war give cause for profound concern, ” reads the text. “ In many countries, hatred and discrimination driven by ideological extremism – including Christian nationalism – have become pervasive, inflicting suffering on diverse social minorities and marginalized communities. ”
The text also names the current context of the Korean Peninsula. “ The two Koreas must find a path to peaceful coexistence grounded in mutual respect, ” reads the text. “ We call for the restoration of communication, the prevention of military incidents, and dialogue among the parties concerned to end the state of war and build a durable peace regime. ”
The document expresses the commitment to promote the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.
“ We stand in solidarity with peoples and communities affected by war, occupation, political violence, and human rights violations, including in Palestine, Ukraine, Myanmar, Sudan, Iran, Sri Lanka, the Philippines, and Colombia, ” reads the text.
The text expresses the commitment to strengthen church-based action for climate justice and the restoration of creation.
“ We understand peace not only as the absence of war but as a process of healing, reconciliation, and transformation, ” reads the text. “ We affirm that peace must be experienced in the everyday lives of people living on the Korean Peninsula. ”
The document also affirms the calling of the churches to become communities of healing and reconciliation in a divided society.
“ We commit ourselves to move from declaration to sustained action, ” reads the text.

articles.title_orig: Inovonics Will Acquire Broadcast Tools Inc.
articles.title_zh: Inovonics Will Acquire Broadcast Tools Inc.
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Business and Law
Broadcast Tools Inc., a manufacturer of specialty and “problem-solving” products for broadcast, will be acquired by Inovonics Broadcast.
Founder and President Donald Winget informed his dealers in a letter on Thursday.
“After nearly 40 years in business, I am finally ready to retire,” he wrote.
BTI is based in Sedro Woolley, Wash. Winget wrote that Inovonics will continue the Broadcast Tools name and product line, moving production to its location in Felton, Calif.
“Ben Barber and his team at Inovonics are fully committed to maintaining the excellence of our products and to nurturing the relationships of trust that have been built with you, our dealers, over these many years.”
BTI products include analog and AES routers, remote controls, satellite channel controllers, analog mixers and DAs, silence monitors and program schedulers.
Winget began in broadcasting as a gofer for the chief engineer of a radio station in Eau Claire, Wis., according to a company history on its website. He served in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam war and later started an engineering contracting business, moving it to the Seattle area in the 1970s. Winget and engineer Lee Hurley created Sentry Systems, an early PC-based automation systems.
Winget founded BTI in 1989 while he was chief engineer at KXRX in Seattle. ( Read a company history .)
Inovonics was founded by Jim Wood and Mark Drake in 1972 to make drop-in, replacement tape recorder electronics assemblies for reel-to-reel machines. The company’s line today includes processors, monitors, RDS products, streaming gear and other specialty broadcast items.

articles.title_orig: Euro Falls to 17-Month Low on Region’s Fiscal, Political Risks
articles.title_zh: Euro Falls to 17-Month Low on Region’s Fiscal, Political Risks
articles.content_orig:
The euro hit its weakest level against the U.S. dollar in 17 months on Monday, as concerns over the political trajectories of two of the euro zone's biggest economies spill over into wider markets.
The eurozone currency was last 0.6% lower against the greenback, hitting its lowest level since May 19, 2025, according to LSEG data.
That comes as the euro zone grapples with a simultaneous rise in inflation , interest rates and government borrowing costs .
The U.S. faces similar pressures, but investors are increasingly unsettled by additional vulnerabilities unique to Europe: persistently weak growth, a fragmented bond market and political uncertainty in Spain and France.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday called a snap election for November , as protests over the country's housing crisis reach boiling point.
The protests have highlighted the difficulty of passing reforms in what has been one of the euro area's bright spots for economic growth in the pandemic rebound.
Rufaro Chiriseri, head of fixed income for RBC Wealth Management, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday that Spanish assets had been among its preferred investments this year because of the country's growth trajectory and relative fiscal stability.
"It's the strength of the commitment to holding some of those fiscal rules that's quite crucial. And even when we did see the [bond market] sell-off last week, and we're looking at Spanish debt, Portuguese debt, it didn't sell off as aggressively as we saw in France, in Italy," Chiriseri said.
"And so that, in a sense, is holding up that investors still think that is an attractive pocket of the market to be in."
France meanwhile remains the "poster child" for Europe's sovereign market problems, as mounting debt piles become more expensive to service.
Economists at Barclays said Friday that while the French government had presented a draft outline of its 2027 budget, aimed at reducing the public deficit from 5.4% of GDP to 5% next year, the country is unlikely meet its fiscal targets even if the plan is adopted in the coming months.
"French fiscal and political developments cloud the euro area outlook, with fiscal fundamentals remaining weak and unlikely to reach an inflection point before next year's presidential election," they said.
Strategists at ING meanwhile said the budget , even if passed in full, would "not resolve France's structural fiscal problems."
"The deficit would remain too high to stabilise the debt ratio, while ageing-related expenditure and interest payments would continue to rise. The next government will therefore have to make further difficult choices," they said.
"So far, none of the main presidential candidates has presented a sufficiently detailed plan explaining which expenditure would be reduced, which taxes would change or how the debt ratio would eventually be stabilised."

articles.title_orig: Two dead, 35 wounded in shooting at Georgia block party
articles.title_zh: Two dead, 35 wounded in shooting at Georgia block party
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: Cornell tipster says she feels ‘betrayed,’ Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague, and trio win Nobel for unraveling the brain’s secrets
Officials were still trying to piece together how a block party left two people dead and 35 others wounded, early Sunday in south-central Georgia.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigation said in a news release that shots were fired at about 1:25 a.m. in Vienna, a rural community about two hours south of Atlanta.
Two men were pronounced dead at the scene.
Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy identified them as JaQuevion Jackson, 21, of Cordele, Georgia; and Macaleb Jackson, 23, of Hawkinsville, Georgia.
The Dooly County coroner, Brett Watts, said they each had a single gunshot wound, though an autopsy by the medical examiner’s office, scheduled for Friday, could provide a fuller picture. He said the men’s families have been notified.
The violence took place at a neighborhood celebration that spanned four blocks, Peavy said at a Sunday night news conference.
The 35 wounded ranged in age from 14 to 51, and were taken to several regional hospitals, he said, adding that their conditions ranged from stable to critical.
“A majority were gunshot victims,” he said.
Deputies were patrolling the party at the time, the sheriff added.
“It was so many people, and it was just hard to figure out what was going on,” Peavy said.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigation declined to say whether authorities had determined a motive or identified a suspect.
The investigation into the shooting was “active and ongoing,” Lydia Bullard, the bureau’s public affairs specialist, said in a statement to NBC News.
The incident took place over homecoming weekend for Dooly County High School.
The shooting was not at a school-sponsored event, said Sherrod Willaford, superintendent of the Dooly County School System.
“We recognize that its impact may reach many of our students, families, and staff,” he said in a statement. Schools will open Monday, he said, but additional safety measures have been put in place. He did not specify what they were.
Peavy said the festivities began Friday night, and that it had “gone well” with “respect from the community” that evening as deputies patrolled the event. But the party Saturday night was a “different story,” he said.
“We’re still working through the investigation to see what went wrong. But at large parties with people from different places, not just your locals, sometimes problems come,” Peavy added.
Aria Bendix is the breaking health reporter for NBC News Digital.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: San Diego Padres vs. Milwaukee Brewers Results, Stats, and Recap - October 4, 2026 Gametracker
articles.title_zh: San Diego Padres vs. Milwaukee Brewers Results, Stats, and Recap - October 4, 2026 Gametracker
articles.content_orig:
MILWAUKEE (AP)  Jackson Chourio says his knack for coming through in clutch situations stems from one instance when he failed to deliver during his rookie year.
Just about every Milwaukee Brewers opponent has been paying for that ever since, as baseball's best closer now knows.
Chourio hit a two-run single off hard-throwing Mason Miller with two outs in the ninth inning as the Brewers rallied past the San Diego Padres for the second straight day, a 4-3 victory Sunday for a 2-0 NL Division Series lead.
“I think it's probably in the top three of the special moments I've had in my career,” Chourio said through interpreter Daniel de Mondesert.
The fact Chourio didn't automatically rank it atop the list speaks volumes about all the memorable moments the 22-year-old already has produced in his first three seasons. Chourio said his drive to deliver in these moments intensified after he struck out against Andrés Muñoz, ending a loss to Seattle early in his rookie year.
“At that point, everything turned for me,” Chourio said. “I told myself I was never going to make the last out. I’d dedicate myself to fighting and doing whatever I could for the team and not having that feeling again from that specific game.”
San Diego, which entered the postseason with 20 wins in its last 23 games, headed home for Game 3 of the best-of-five series on Tuesday following its first back-to-back losses since Sept. 1-2.
Milwaukee rallied from 2-0 deficits on consecutive days by beating the Padres' bullpen. William Contreras hit a tiebreaking homer in the seventh inning against Adrian Morejon on Saturday.
“It’s a big challenge,” Padres manager Craig Stammen said. “They’re a great team. You saw how hard they battle us here in Milwaukee. But we like where we are when we play at home."
Michael King retired his first 14 batters as the Padres went ahead 2-0, and they led 3-2 when Miller entered trying for his first six-out save since 2024.
The two-time All-Star closer retired the side in order in the eighth. After a leadoff groundout in the ninth, Miller issued his first career postseason walks to Christian Yelich and Sal Frelick.
Andrew Vaughn flied out and pinch hitter Gary Sánchez walked, taking six straight pitches.
That brought Chourio to the plate, one day after he sparked a 4-3 comeback victory with a tying, two-run homer in the third inning.
“Watching those at-bats beforehand, I knew that he was a little bit erratic,” Chourio said. “He was throwing some balls. I knew that he was going to come at me with the fastball at some point, so mentally I was just making sure that I was prepared for that.”
Chourio connected on a 2-2 pitch, lining a 101.3 mph fastball up the middle and past second baseman Jake Cronenworth’s attempt for a diving backhand stop. Cronenworth believed he was inches away from making the play.
“He smashed it, but I thought I got a good jump on it,” Cronenworth said.
The ball bounced into center field as Yelich ran across the plate. Frelick slid in head first, easily beating center fielder Jackson Merrill’s throw.
Miller threw a season-high 40 pitches - his most since 2023 - but said after the game that didn't impact him. He topped 100 mph with 18 pitches, the fastest a 103.5 mph offering that Chourio fouled.
"I didn’t do my job today, so instead of being here with a win and a series tie, we’re in a hole," Miller said.
At 22 years, 207 days, Chourio became the second-youngest player with a postseason walk-off hit. Edgar Renteria was 22 years old but younger than Chourio is today when he had two walk-off hits during the Florida Marlins' run to the 1997 World Series title.
Chourio has hit .327 with a franchise-record five homers to go along with 15 RBIs in 14 career postseason games.
“He loves those moments,” Yelich said. “And he knows how talented he is and what he can do on a baseball field. He can do anything.”
Chourio also made a key defensive play in the opener when Ty France hit a potential go-ahead homer in the ninth inning only for the ball to strike a cable on the roof of American Family Field and land in the left fielder's glove at the warning track.
With the roof open Sunday, France hit an RBI single in the first and another a run-scoring single for a 3-1 lead in the seventh after third baseman David Hamilton bobbled Fernando Tatis Jr.'s grounder for an error.
Frelick had an RBI single in the fifth after Christian Yelich doubled.
Milwaukee closed to 3-2 in the seventh when Garrett Mitchell scored from third as Cronenworth bobbled Hamilton's grounder and then threw past first for a double error.
“We could very easily be going home up 2-0,” France said. “But the reality is we're not. We have to go and we have to win. No ifs, ands or buts, we have to play our best baseball now.”

articles.title_orig: China expands its military base network in Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: China expands its military base network in Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
Hong Kong, October 5 (ANI): China’s first overseas military base was set up in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in 2017, but it now also has access to two bases in Southeast Asia. One is a naval facility in Cambodia, and the latest revelation is of a newly built air base in neighbouring Laos.
The news of the Laos base came as a surprise, with China’s Ministry of National Defense (MND) revealing its existence on 29 September 2026. It stated on social media that “the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport in Laos and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy officially went into operation”.
An official ceremony was graced by Laotian Defense Minister Khamlieng Outhakayson. Incidentally, the opening of the new base comes after Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith visited Beijing to meet Chairman Xi Jinping in June. On that occasion, Xi called for strategic dialogue on a number of issues, such as national defence.
With grid coordinates of 18.36043°N 102.56424°E, this air base in Ban Keun is approximately 50km north of the Laotian capital, Vientiane. The airfield was once home to Lima Site 44, part of a network of airbases built by the US military and CIA during the Vietnam War. Laos is one of the poorest countries in Asia.
The site was converted from farmland, and construction seemed to start late last year. The base features a 2,000m-long paved runway, as well as a taxiway, a parking apron, an air traffic control tower, and five hangars at its northern end. Most of the supporting infrastructure is in place, although works are still ongoing.
The MND’s announcement continued: “The two institutions, jointly maintained and operated by both sides, aim to help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots. The establishment and operation of the two institutions reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, aligning with domestic laws of both countries, as well as international law and common practices.”
China’s military said the base is “not directed against any third party" and that it “aims to help further deepen practical cooperation between the two militaries and contribute to maintaining peace and stability in the region."
As for not being directed against a “third party”, the country most alarmed by this development will be Vietnam. China instigated an invasion of Vietnam in 1979. This airbase gives the PLA a foothold some 400km farther south into the Indochina Peninsula than its existing southwestern border. The location is also due west of Vietnam. This means China can use it to exert influence deep in Indochina.
The Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force (LPLAAF) is small, comprising a mix of Russian-built and Chinese-built aircraft and helicopters. Sourced from China, the air force possesses single MA60 and MA600 transport aircraft, four Z-9 helicopters, five LE500 turboprop basic trainers and a quartet of K-8W jet trainers/light attack aircraft. The LPLAAF has two primary air bases: one is at Vientiane-Wattay International Airport, and the other at Xiengkhouang to the northeast.
With such a diminutive air force, it would appear the LPLAAF’s training requirements are not great. Of course, China will be keen to wean Laos off Russian equipment entirely and to supply its own aircraft and weapons. Such a move creates long-term dependencies, which will enable Beijing to exert further pressure.
In typical fashion, China did not disclose what assets, aircraft platforms or personnel numbers would deploy to Laos. However, one source suggested the People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) will base JL-8 jet trainers at the new Ban Keun facility, alongside relocated Laotian K-8Ws.
A key question is the legal arrangements and terms governing PLA access to Ben Keun Air Base. Presumably the PLA needs the host’s permission to use the airfield outside of any existing commitments, though this does not prevent Beijing from putting pressure on Vientiane to achieve its wishes.
The China-Global South Project (CGSP) quoted Junwu Ciweimian, the author of a popular Chinese military commentary account. He cited two reasons for the PLA choosing to set up at Ban Keun. “First is transportation. Ban Keun lies along the China-Laos Railway corridor, making it easier to move personnel and equipment from China. Second is geography. Ban Keun is close to the capital, making it convenient for trainees and easier for the Lao government to manage. The surrounding area is also relatively flat, compared with much of mountainous Laos, making it better suited for an airfield and flight training.”
Junwu also identified three purposes for the facility. The first is training the LPLAAF, and providing ample room for China to exert influence. “With the establishment of the joint aviation academy, the course is essentially set for the Lao air force’s future equipment to become fully Chinese-made.”
Secondly, CGSP quoted: “China already regularly conducts air exercises in the region, including annual joint drills with Thailand. Ban Keun could provide another operating location for Chinese aircraft. Rather than moving every aircraft directly to Thailand, the account suggested, China could leave some at Ban Keun and conduct exercises using two bases, making the training ‘closer to actual combat’.”
The third reason relates to regional influence. “Ban Keun also occupies a favourable strategic position. Several important cities in mainland Southeast Asia are roughly 500 to 700 kilometres away, while even the more distant ones are only a little over 1,000 kilometres from the facility. Establishing a support base there, it said, would be useful for China to ‘exert influence in the Indochina Peninsula in the future’.”
In similar vein, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute made this assessment: “There are no details available about what Chinese personnel, equipment or capabilities will be based there. Ban Keun’s operational value isn’t obvious, given the Chinese military can already operate from neighbouring Yunnan. Its significance may instead lie in establishing a persistent military presence in Laos and deepening ties with Lao armed forces.”
The CGSP also quoted another Chinese commentator, Rongping, who asserted this Lao base represents a different model than the PLA’s Djibouti and Cambodian facilities. This is true, for the Djibouti base primarily supports Chinese anti-piracy naval task groups operating in the Gulf of Aden. Of course, there is more to it than that, for the facility hosts a strong contingent of PLA Navy marines equipped with armoured vehicles, for instance. This gives the PLA a rapid reaction force in the Horn of Africa, able to respond quickly to crises in Africa or the nearby Middle East. The Djibouti base is also used to train PLA peacekeeping troops deploying to Africa.
Regarding Djibouti, the Pentagon, however, assessed that the Djibouti base has had minimal involvement in protecting Chinese citizens or investments, which was actually a stated purpose of the facility. The USA stated: “To date, the support base has not supported non-combatant evacuations and has not provided support to the ongoing Red Sea crisis. Instead, the facility has enabled persistent PLA regional presence under the auspices of support to counter-piracy and increasingly supports regional military diplomacy.”
The key difference about the Laos facility is that it is the first air force-specific base for the PLA outside China. The Chinese military will presumably rotate forces into the base, as well as maintain a forward-support presence there. This means the PLA will have a permanent and persistent presence in Laos.
Rongping also wondered whether China chose Laos only because Cambodia might have said no to such a facility on its own territory. Phnom Penh does not want to throw in its lot entirely with China, and it is hedging with the likes of the USA and Japan. Cambodia receives official security assistance from Japan, for instance.

Marex has won World’s Best FX Provider for Client Service at the Euromoney Foreign Exchange Awards 2026, recognizing our approach to client service for corporate treasury and institutional clients across both Corporate FX and Hedging Solutions, and its position as a non-bank challenger in a category historically dominated by global banks.
The award, typically presented as World’s Best Bank for Client Service, was adapted to reflect Marex’s profile as a non-bank financial services platform.
The recognition caps a period of rapid growth for Marex’s Corporate FX business. Following the acquisition of Hamilton Court Group in July 2025, Marex’s FX revenue grew 362% in 2025 to $66.1 million, up from $14.3 million in 2024 (Marex Group 2025 Annual Report).
Marex’s approach to client service pairs specialist treasury expertise with institutional-grade market access, combining relationship-led advisory with proprietary technology. Neon, Marex’s client portal, brings together the Emporos and MIRA platforms acquired with Hamilton Court Group, giving clients a single view of risk profiling, hedge analytics, trading and reporting. AGILE, Marex’s award-winning platform for managing commodity and currency hedging portfolios, sits alongside it.
“At Marex, exceptional client service starts with understanding each client’s business and objectives, then designing the right solution. Hamilton Court’s 2025 integration deepened that expertise, resulting in a responsive, connected proposition that helps clients manage risk in complex markets, execute with confidence and access a broader range of tailored solutions.”
Greg Tsimbler, Deputy CEO of Capital Markets and Global Head of FX & Payments, Marex
The win adds to a strong year of industry recognition for Marex’s FX business, which has also been named Best Service from a Business FX Provider at the Business Moneyfacts Awards for four consecutive years (2023–2026). articles.title_orig: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.title_zh: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil exports from the Middle East have risen above pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed.
However, senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview on Sunday night that only three to four million barrels of oil per day (bpd) are now moving through the route, dismissing the amount as “negligible” when compared with pre-war traffic.
Fadavi said, for the first time, no US vessels were present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean and US warships are “100 percent vulnerable” to IRGC attacks.
Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd.
Around that time, Iran claimed success in attacking ships – including US Navy vessels – near the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strikes had forced Washington to move its warships further from the Iranian coast.
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began, exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February 2026.
According to Kpler data, the overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30.
On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd. This includes transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
The number of liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the Strait of Hormuz also rose in September to its highest monthly level since February.
The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or in the Gulf of Aden since October 2.
On Sunday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway.

articles.title_orig: Particle physicist Hideki Yukawa: Japan’s first Nobel laureate
articles.title_zh: Particle physicist Hideki Yukawa: Japan’s first Nobel laureate
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
While modern Japan has had a good record in winning Nobel prizes, the country had to wait 48 years since the inception of the awards in 1901 to receive its first Nobel prize.
The accolade went to particle physicist Hideki Yukawa , who published his theory of mesons in the 1930s that explained the interaction between protons and neutrons.
Yukawa was born in  Tokyo on 23 January 1907, graduating from Kyoto University in 1929. He then moved to Osaka University in 1933 for a PhD, which is where he did his Nobel-prize-winning work.
As positively charged protons repel each other through electromagnetic force, an issue at the time in nuclear physics was that this should cause the atomic nucleus to fly apart.
In 1935 Yukawa proposed a short-range, highly attractive nuclear force that overcomes this repulsion and suggested this force is created by the exchange of massive subatomic particles between protons and neutrons, which he called mesons.
Yukawa calculated that the mass of these exchange particles should be roughly between an electron and a proton.
In 1937 three separate research groups conducted cloud-chamber experiments and discovered a new particle with a mass consistent with Yukawa’s prediction, but it was later identified as a muon.
In 1938 Yukawa was awarded a PhD and a year later moved back to Kyoto University but it took a few more years before Yukawa’s particle was finally discovered.
The first evidence of a meson came in 1947 with the discovery of the pi meson (pion) by a research group led by Cecil Powell at the University of Bristol. The team measured the particle by exposing photographic plates to cosmic rays at high altitudes ( Powell won the 1950 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work ).
Yukawa was then awarded the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physics “for his prediction of the existence of mesons on the basis of theoretical work on nuclear forces”.
The news was met with tremendous joy in Japan and encouraged scientists to continue their research in spite of the economic condition and the challenges of doing experimental science in postwar Japan. Revitalizing Japanese physics Read more
Revitalizing Japanese physics
In Yukawa’s honour, the Japanese government built a three-storey building named Yukawa Hall in 1952. Its focus was on developing theoretical physics in Japan and featured lecture halls, seminar rooms, offices and a library.
In 1953 the hall became home to the Research Institute for Fundamental Physics (now the Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics ), of which Yukawa was the first director – a position he held until retiring in 1970.
The institute invited research scholars from all over Japan and held symposia and seminars on particle physics. It also published the monthly English-language journal Progress of Theoretical Physics (now known as Progress of Theoretical and Experimental Physics ), together with the Physical Society of Japan (JPS).
The journal was founded by Yukawa in 1946 to publish results that had remained unpublished because of JPS’s financial difficulties.
As well as the Nobel prize, Yukawa also won many other international prizes and he was also vocal about issues in physics and society. In 1955 Yukawa joined 10 other scientists in signing the Russell–Einstein Manifesto that called for nuclear disarmament.
Yukawa died on 8 September 1981 and since he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics, 11 other Japanese-born physicists have gone on to win the physics Nobel – making Japan one of the most successful countries in the world.

articles.title_orig: Karl review – straightforward tribute tells inside story of fashion world’s great eccentric Karl Lagerfeld
articles.title_zh: Karl review – straightforward tribute tells inside story of fashion world’s great eccentric Karl Lagerfeld
articles.content_orig:
Based on Lagerfeld’s biography, director Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately fails to find the man behind the high collar and sunglasses
K arl Lagerfeld had never set foot inside a supermarket before he had one built on a catwalk in 2014, featuring models browsing aisles with baskets shopping for Chanel-branded fromage. It was classic Lagerfeld: very silly but a stroke of genius. The fashion designer was easy to poke fun at, with his white bouffant-plus-ponytail hairstyle and black leather gloves. But behind the persona was a man who spoke four languages fluently, a workaholic still running Chanel, Fendi and his own label Karl Lagerfeld into his 80s.
This dutiful, uncontroversial documentary is based on William Middleton’s biography Paradise Now: The Extraordinary Life of Karl Lagerfeld . As well as archive footage of Lagerfeld, film-maker Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately his documentary fails to chip away at the persona. (This is no criticism: I once interviewed Lagerfeld, a frustrating 30 minutes during which the dark glasses stayed on and he answered questions with bon mot witticisms but gave nothing away.) In a clip at the start of the film, Lagerfeld admits that he has spent so long performing a role that not even those closest to him really know who he is.
Growing up in Germany, his mother was cold and distant, which seems to have left him with a life-long aversion to intimacy. At 19, he left for Paris, and after a long stint at Chloé took over Chanel in 1983, at a time when the legendary fashion house was dusty and on its uppers. He lost the great love of his life, partner Jacques de Bascher, to an Aids-related illness in 1989. Later in life, his smash hit collaboration with H&M gave Lagerfeld celebrity status, which he clearly adored. But glance away and you’ll miss the very quick reference to his controversial fatphobic comments .
Of the interviews here, Lagerfeld’s famous pals Tilda Swinton and Penélope Cruz are all blather and platitudes, but more insightful are his collaborators, including Amanda Harlech, his right-hand woman at Chanel . I found it telling how well liked Lagerfeld was by his staff; the seamstress who worked for him for 50 years turning his sketches into clothes describes him as “the crème de la crème of men”. His longtime bodyguard says he was like a father. (Though, if Lagerfeld had actually been his dad there were times he’d have told him to “go fuck yourself”.) Overall, this is a diligent, if not definitive, profile.

articles.title_orig: Tennessee’s outgoing prison chief had a history of execution missteps before Christa Pike, officials say
articles.title_zh: Tennessee’s outgoing prison chief had a history of execution missteps before Christa Pike, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Before the botched execution of Christa Pike, Frank Strada reportedly had a history of overseeing execution missteps in two states.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee on Saturday announced Correction Commissioner Strada would step down later this month following the backlash after the attempted execution left Pike on a ventilator, unconscious in a hospital. Less than three years earlier, Lee brought Strada on to lead the Department of Correction, tasking him with reforming Tennessee’s execution system after enduring concerns over the state’s approach to the death penalty.
But in Strada’s previous role as an official in Arizona’s prisons system, he oversaw three executions that administrators and observers raised concerns over, saying executioners flouted the state’s official policies. Now under his current supervision, Pike is the second person this year who Tennessee officials have failed to execute after problems with the IV injections.
The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment when asked by CNN about Strada’s involvement in these prior execution problems.
Pike’s debilitating survival has brought to light Strada’s history overseeing executions that didn’t follow typical protocol, and larger questions about the death penalty by both proponents and opponents. Lee has suspended executions for the year as an investigation is underway.
“The state of Tennessee has got to start telling its people exactly what it is doing, so that in the democratic process, the people of Tennessee can decide if that’s what they want to be done in their name,” Stephen Ferrell, Pike’s lawyer, told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Sunday. “This torturous execution leaves so many questions that the state of Tennessee will refuse to answer.”
As his resignation was announced, Strada said, “stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward.”
“I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary,” Strada said in a statement Saturday, “and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.”
Here’s the latest on Strada’s final days overseeing Tennessee’s prisons, and what happened inside Pike’s death chamber.
On Saturday, the state Attorney General’s Office retained Ed Stanton, a former US attorney, to conduct an independent review of the Department of Correction’s actions in carrying out Pike’s execution, Gov. Lee’s office announced.
Stanton previously oversaw an independent review of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol in 2022, the governor’s office said, which resulted in the state substantially rewriting its protocol.
Strada began leading Tennessee’s correction department in 2023 when he was tasked with enacting that new protocol among other duties. An Air Force veteran, Strada was a senior official in Arizona’s prison system who previously had worked nearly 30 years for the Federal Bureau of Prisons.
In naming Strada to lead the agency , Lee said Strada’s “extensive corrections management and law enforcement experience make him well-suited to lead the Department of Correction.”
Strada served as a deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry. His tenure was marked with controversy around three executions that were performed after an eight-year moratorium in the state.
All three had issues with establishing IV lines to administer the lethal drug, lawyers said. The problems prompted Arizona’s governor to call for an independent review of execution protocols. The review in Arizona was announced weeks after Lee promoted Strada to his current post in Tennessee.
In a 2023 sworn declaration, Ryan Thornell, director of Arizona’s corrections department, said he was “unable to locate sufficient documentation” about execution procedures under the previous administration, which included Strada. He cited “several critical issues” impacting the agency’s ability to conduct executions, including inadequate expertise, efficacy of lethal injection drugs, and procedures with the IV team.
Thornell said he couldn’t find documentation identifying the pharmacist who compounded the lethal drugs. Without naming Strada, he said a prior deputy director was the main point of contact with the pharmacist but said he didn’t record anything. The effectiveness of the current supplies of the lethal drug couldn’t be guaranteed and needed to be tested to ensure safety and efficacy prior to use, Thornell said.
Meanwhile, he said the IV team who worked on the state’s most recent execution had been told by the prior administration to only use the femoral central line, which was against the department’s policy.
In Tennessee, questions have mounted around the Department of Correction’s protocol around executions, including IV administration to administer lethal doses.
Pike’s case wasn’t the first time state officials had trouble with lethal injections in recent months. In May, state officials halted the execution of Tony Carruthers when staff couldn’t get a secondary IV successfully placed after placing one IV into his right arm.
Later, the state’s execution of Anthony Darrell Hines was performed in August without any reported issues with placing the IVs, according to The Associated Press.
Advocates said issues with Tennessee’s procedures speak to larger issues around the death penalty.
“It’s not isolated to just one particular person or one particular execution team,” Kat Jutras, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Alternatives for Arizona, told CNN. “If we look at it in that very microlens, we’re not seeing the broader picture with the death penalty itself and lethal injections really being at the forefront of some of the larger problems.”
Pike, who along with her boyfriend was convicted for the 1995 torture and killing of her classmate Colleen Slemmer, was one of the youngest women sent to death row.
During her scheduled execution Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, executioners struggled to set the IV lines necessary to administer the lethal dose of pentobarbital. Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, told reporters she cooperated with the execution team and tried to give them tips on how to insert the IV lines, as she had warned the state she had a history with difficult vein access.
But her lawyers said issues with the IV resulted in the barbiturate, which slows the central nervous system, flowing into her body instead of her bloodstream. After the first dose failed to work, executioners administered a second dose.
“We may never know what sort of torture she endured during that process,” Ferrell, an assistant federal defender in Tennessee, said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” It’s unclear whether she was conscious or in physical pain during the procedure and subsequent life-saving treatment, he added.
“We don’t know what the prognosis is, as in the long-term prognosis, if she recovers,” he said, saying she remained unconscious in the hospital as of Sunday morning. “She may not fully recover.”
Her lawyers have called on the governor to commute Pike’s death sentence. After being convicted of first-degree murder, Pike has served more than 30 years in prison, mostly in solitary confinement, only to be brought out for a failed execution, Ferrell said.
“This has been a serious punishment for a very serious and awful crime,” Ferrell said. “I don’t think that attempting another execution is going to bring justice.”
The state Attorney General’s Office hasn’t given an indication of whether they’ll seek to put her to death again, he added.
Gov. Lee, who is term-limited after serving for eight years, will leave office in January. Republican US Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who is running to replace him, has called to bring back the electric chair to “deliver justice for these victims swiftly.”
Some Tennessee lawmakers, including state House Speaker Cameron Sexton , have also proposed allowing the firing squad as an alternative execution method. At least five states have authorized the use

articles.title_orig: An Invitation From the Prophet to the World
articles.title_zh: An Invitation From the Prophet to the World
articles.content_orig:
In his closing remarks during the Sunday afternoon session of general conference on October 4, 2026, President Dallin H. Oaks of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints invited the world to participate in the Salt Lake Temple Celebration, either in person or virtually.
As part of his special invitation, President Oaks highlighted a new video series. “Following this session of general conference, the first episode of a dynamic video series, ‘Dedicate,’ will premiere worldwide in multiple languages,” he said. “More will come in the months ahead, including a virtual tour of the Salt Lake Temple.”
“Dedicate” follows seven young adults from Brazil, France, Ghana, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines and the United States as they explore the Salt Lake Temple, meet with Church leaders and navigate questions of faith, purpose and spiritual growth. Throughout the series, they share personal experiences as they deepen their understanding of temples and strengthen their faith in Jesus Christ.
The first episode is now available on the Church’s YouTube channel and will be added to the Gospel Library app in the coming days.
Four additional “Dedicate” episodes will be released every Sunday at 8 a.m. MDT through November 1, with the sixth and final episode set to air in spring 2027. In addition to English, episodes are available in Cantonese, Chinese (Traditional), French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish.
For the first time since 1893, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will open the doors of the newly renovated Salt Lake Temple. The public is invited to experience the beauty of this sacred space from April 5, 2027, to October 1, 2027. This significant six-month event is for everyone, whether they participate in person on Temple Square or from elsewhere in the world through virtual experiences.
The celebration will include the open house tour, exhibits, performances, films, service opportunities, and other experiences centered on the Savior of the world. During the celebration, guests will also find opportunities to enjoy live music, exhibits, and other events. articles.title_orig: WCC general secretary shares encouragement with WCC education commission
articles.title_zh: WCC general secretary shares encouragement with WCC education commission
articles.content_orig:
In a special message entitled “ The Spirit of Ecumenical Learning,” World Council of Churches (WCC) general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay shared appreciation for the work of the WCC Ecumenical Education and Formation Commission as they start their biannual meeting at the WCC Ecumenical Institute at Bossey.
WCC general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay addressed the opening session of the EEF Commission via video message. He will join the group on 7 October for the celebrations of the 80th anniversary of the WCC Ecumenical Institute at Bossey.
“ As you gather here in these days, I appreciate all of you for traveling long distances to confer about the state of ecumenical education globally and to advance the cause of ecumenical education and formation,” wrote Pillay.
“ After the celebrations and deliberations in Egypt last year of the 1700th anniversary of the Nicene Creed, our theological imperative is clearer than ever: we are called to critical appropriation of that ancient, life-giving faith in every context to face and address our global crisis at its deepest spiritual level.”
Pillay noted that ecumenical learning liberates us from our parochial thinking and frees us to throw ourselves into that work with open minds and hearts, wherever we are.
“ Discerning the will of God in these changing and challenging times is essential so that we may bring glory to God and relevantly address the needs of our times,” he wrote. “ So, dear commissioners, my hopes and prayers are with you as you gather these days.”
The EEF Commission meeting goes from 5-9 October, bringing together members for a week of reflection, evaluation, and planning around the future of ecumenical education and formation.
Under the theme “Ecumenical Formation as Ethos and as Programme,” the meeting will consider the commission’s mandate and priorities, review current initiatives, and identify directions for its future work.
