articles.title_orig: Gaorong closes $486M fund as industrial capital floods China's VCs
articles.title_zh: Gaorong closes $486M fund as industrial capital floods China's VCs
articles.content_orig:
What's the deal? Gaorong Ventures has completed fundraising for its Tianjin Gaorong Changying Fund, securing 3.261 billion CNY (about $486 million) in committed capital. The venture fund drew heavily from China's traditional industrial sectors rather than the usual tech-focused backers.
Who's backing it? Junzheng Group and its wholly-owned subsidiary committed 1 billion CNY, more than 30% of the total. Pig farmer Muyuan Industrial added 350 million CNY, Zijin Mining entities 300 million CNY, Jiahua Energy 200 million CNY, and Newland Digital Technology 100 million CNY — capital from chemicals, agriculture, and mining pooled into one market-oriented fund.
Why now? Gaorong's close lands amid a broader rebound. Fundraising in China's primary market is recovering, with 3,981 new funds raised in the first half of 2026 totalling 1,049.464 billion CNY — up 95.8% and 49.6% year-on-year, respectively.
The bigger shift: State-owned capital has anchored the market for years, but industrial capital's move into market-oriented funds is newer. Wuyuan , Matrix Partners China , and Lisi have all advanced new offerings with similar backers.
Who else is in? Wuyuan's new fund drew 100 million CNY from Xiaomi -linked Hanxing Venture Capital , plus entities tied to Liu Qiangdong and TAL Education . Zhihu plans to put 1.5 billion CNY into Lisi's Xingshen Fund. Matrix Partners' Chuangyi Future Fund targets 7 billion CNY and has secured 3.72123 billion CNY so far, with SF Express , East Money , and Vipshop among its backers.
The signal: Industrial giants — once cautious — are now writing large cheques to tech investors, reshaping who funds China's startups. GPs that pair strong track records with deal-sourcing strength are winning the new money.

articles.title_orig: Crowds gather in Spain for world's biggest human tower contest
articles.title_zh: Crowds gather in Spain for world's biggest human tower contest
articles.content_orig:
Published: 18:43 EDT, 4 October 2026 | Updated: 21:03 EDT, 4 October 2026
Thousands have gathered at a Spanish arena to watch a near-century-old competition which sees teams battle to build the tallest human tower.
Held every two years in an ancient bullfighting ring in Tarragona, the castells competition sees human tower groups from across Catalonia gather to face off.
Some teams built towers of eight human storeys over the weekend, with the Marrecs de Salt team winning Saturday's competition in the Tarraco Arena.
Teams of up to 500 men, women and children compete to build the tallest tower in the exhibition - which can be as many as ten levels tall.
The highest and most complicated tower is dubbed the winner, with some reaching over 40ft tall in recent years.
This year's edition was the competition's 30th outing since its first staging in 1932.
Teams competed in Catalonia's Castells event, which challenged competitors to build the tallest human towers
Held every two years, the competition has been staged 30 times since its inaugural outing in 1932. Pictured: the Castellers de Barcelona team forming a tower
But the Castellers de Barcelona tower collapsed into itself as the red-shirted participants tumbled over
Castells are human towers, which can reach up to ten people tall or over 40ft high
Thousands gathered at the Tarraco Arena, west of Barcelona, to witness the face off
Towers rose out of the crowded arena floor as teams vied to produce the tallest castell
Members of one pink-clad team, the Castellers Joves de Valls, collapsed as their tower failed on Sunday
But others were more successful in the near-century-old Catalonian competition
Members of Castellers Colla Vella wearing red uniforms banded together to form a human tower
Crumbling towers are not uncommon in the competition, as the Castellers Joves de Valls showed
A sea of blue-clad members of the Colla Castellera de Sant Pere i Sant Pau team begin to form a tower
Members of the Castellers Joves de Valls reacted to another team's effort to form a tower this weekend
Originating at the end of the 18th century, castells can be spotted outside the competition in Catalonia's cities and town squares.
In 1867 the choral tune Els Xiquets de Valls by Josep Anselm Clave said 'strength, balance, courage and good judgment' were the key ingredients for a successful tower.
Generally teams work outside competitive spaces to push their own limits, with the Tarragona contest a rare exception.
Castells need a minimum of six levels to be considered as such and each level has its own name.
At the top is the crowner, who signals the tower's completion by raising their arm at the end of its construction.
According to Europeana teams can have any number of members from 100 to 1,000.
Teams are recognisable by their uniforms and are often named for their place of origin, for example Xiquets de Valls, Marrecs de Salt and Castellers de Barcelona.

Skyworks Solutions, Inc. (SWKS) and Qorvo Inc. (QRVO) will move to combine on Monday and create a $22 billion high-performance RF, analog and mixed-signal solutions company.

articles.title_orig: US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
articles.title_zh: US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
articles.content_orig:
The United States has made the abrupt decision to withdraw its bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford in the western part of the United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack.
Media reports emerged on Sunday that an urgent redeployment was under way, with B-1 bombers leaving RAF Fairford for the US.
Roughly a dozen such aircraft had been based at RAF Fairford prior to the sudden departure.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime,” the official added.
It is unclear precisely what prompted the withdrawal, which comes as the US and Israel remain embroiled in a war against Iran.
RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.
But the base, located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Iran.
On September 27, UK authorities arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near the base.
Iran has denied any such scheme, and the men were released without charge a day later. Investigators discovered petrol, but no explosive devices, in their vans. Still, officials in the UK say they remain under investigation.
On Thursday, British police also announced they had arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack against the airbase.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot, though he declined to provide details.
“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said in a statement.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
US President Donald Trump responded to the initial arrests by accusing the men of seeking to do “big damage” to US facilities. He also praised UK authorities for their efforts.
“The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain – it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation,” Trump said of the suspects. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”
Iran, meanwhile, summoned the UK ambassador to Tehran over the last week in protest of the arrests.
The US has a long history of stationing forces at RAF Fairford during its wars in the Middle East, stretching back to the Gulf War in the 1990s.
RAF Fairford has been the site of antiwar protests in the past. During one instance, in 2003, five protesters broke into the airbase in an attempt to destroy military equipment slated to be used in the US invasion of Iraq.
The UK has largely declined to participate in the ongoing war on Iran, despite pressure from the Trump administration.
Still, while the UK government was initially hesitant to let the US use its bases for the war, it granted the US “defensive” access to bases, including Fairford and RAF Diego Garcia, in March.

articles.title_orig: Monday is World Teachers’ Day, honoring educators and marking 60-year milestone
articles.title_zh: Monday is World Teachers’ Day, honoring educators and marking 60-year milestone
articles.content_orig:
BEND, Ore. (KTVZ) -- Students and families across Central Oregon can join people around the world Monday in recognizing the educators who help children learn, grow, and prepare for their futures.
World Teachers’ Day is observed each year on October 5th to celebrate teachers and draw attention to the support, training, and working conditions they need to succeed.
The date commemorates the adoption of the 1966 International Labour Organization and UNESCO Recommendation Concerning the Status of Teachers. The landmark document established international standards related to teacher preparation, recruitment, employment, professional development, rights, and responsibilities.
This year’s observance marks the recommendation’s 60th anniversary. The 2026 theme is “Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures.”
UNESCO says this year’s events will examine challenges affecting the status of teachers and call on communities and policymakers to protect, promote, and elevate the profession.
Teachers’ influence often extends well beyond lessons in reading, writing, math, and science. Educators also help students build confidence, explore career paths, solve problems, and navigate important stages of their lives.
For Central Oregon families, Monday offers a simple opportunity to thank a teacher, counselor, or other school employee who has made a difference.

articles.title_orig: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.title_zh: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.content_orig:
Climate change could make a number of infectious diseases worse. I expected malaria would be one of them.
That’s concerning, given the huge global burden that it already carries: it kills almost half a million children every year.
But a more complex story emerges from the scientific literature. One where rising temperatures could actually reduce the burden of malaria in some areas, while making it worse in others.
What impact has climate change already had on malaria? Will it make the global fight against it harder or easier in the future?
These are the questions that I want to answer here.
Before we look at how climate change could change the dynamics and distribution of malaria in the future, we need a quick primer on the global burden of the disease today.
This is important because climate change could cause a decline in malaria in some regions, while increasing the prevalence in others. The impact on the overall global burden of malaria will mostly depend on what happens in the worst-affected regions today.
Malaria is an infectious disease present across much of the tropics and subtropics. In the map below, you can see the band of new infections across South America, South and Southeast Asia, and Africa.
The difference between sub-Saharan Africa and other parts of the tropics, though, is huge. Infection rates in sub-Saharan Africa are around 100 times higher than in South America and 50 times higher than in South Asia.
The fact that severe malaria is mostly an African story today is even clearer when we look at where people die from it. More than 95% of the 600,000 people who die from malaria every year live in sub-Saharan Africa. You can see this regional breakdown below. 1
But this chart also makes clear that within sub-Saharan Africa, there are substantial differences in the burden.
Around half of global deaths occur in West Africa — countries like Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Liberia. The rest are split between the central and eastern parts of the continent. Southern Africa has extremely low rates of malaria.
This dominance in West Africa is not just about population (we might expect more deaths in denser areas). As you can see in this map of death rates , those living in West Africa are at a much higher risk of dying from malaria.
These are the important background facts to make sense of this article’s focus. Most deaths from malaria occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Within the continent, West Africa is hit the worst. And children are most at risk: tragically, around 70% of malaria deaths are among children. That’s almost half a million children dying of the disease every year.
To understand the link between malaria and climate change, we need to know the basics of the disease’s “perfect conditions”.
Several mosquito species in Africa carry and spread malaria. A dominant one is Anopheles gambiae . It carries and spreads the parasite Plasmodium falciparum , which is what infects humans.
Over many decades, scientists have studied the ideal conditions for these mosquitoes to thrive. The spread of malaria peaks in these species at around 25°C. 2 Transmission drops close to zero below 16°C and above 34°C.
That means the suitability of malaria forms a bell-shaped curve like the one below. It spreads best at 25°C; this suitability drops on either side of it, and eventually becomes negligible.
Temperature is not the only thing that matters. How established malaria already is in a given country or region does, too. As do rainfall patterns: female mosquitoes lay their eggs in standing water, and larvae need water to develop. So, rainfall creates favorable conditions for malaria to spread. There is a limit, though: heavy, persistent rain often washes larvae away, preventing them from developing. An area with moderate rainfall is therefore a good breeding ground for malaria to spread.
Humidity can also have an effect. Adult Anopheles dry out in low-humidity air, so they often live longer in wetter, more humid seasons (and when they live longer, they do a better job of spreading the parasite).
The world has already warmed by around 1.4°C since pre-industrial times. 3
What impact has this already had on the prevalence of malaria?
A recent paper by Colin Carlson and colleagues, published in Nature , estimated the impact of historical climate change on the burden of malaria so far, and projected how this might affect it in the future under different warming scenarios. 4 The paper focused on the burden on children in Africa — as we established earlier, this is the most affected demographic, both in terms of cases and deaths.
They estimate that over the last century — from 1901 to 2014 — climate change has led to a small increase in the prevalence of childhood malaria across sub-Saharan Africa. By “increase”, they mean that rates were slightly higher than they would have been compared to a hypothetical scenario without climate change . The prevalence of malaria has actually declined in recent decades, but for reasons unrelated to climate.
Across the region, this increase was estimated at roughly 1 case per 1,000 children aged 2 to 10. To put this into context, around 24% of children (or 240 in every 1,000) in this region were estimated to carry the malaria parasite at the end of the study period. So, the overall impact has been relatively small and is quite uncertain. 59% of the study’s simulations showed an increase in malaria prevalence, with uncertainty ranging from a reduction of 4 cases per 1,000 to an increase of 6 cases per 1,000.
The bigger impact has been in changing the prevalence of malaria across different parts of the continent. Hotter temperatures might not have led to a large increase, on average, but they have affected its distribution.
Climate change has probably led to a decline in malaria in West Africa, but an increase in the southern and eastern parts of the continent. The following map summarizes this change: you see blue in the West but red, marking an increase, in the East and South.
Remember that West Africa is where the burden of malaria has been, and still is, the highest. A decline there due to climate change has been almost entirely offset by an increase elsewhere on the continent, which is why the effect, on aggregate, is very small.
The chart below shows malaria prevalence in two scenarios: the realistic one the world has lived through, and an alternate reality without human-driven climate change. Malaria has declined in West Africa due to climate change, but has increased in the other three subregions.
To understand why climate change has made things better in West Africa, but worse elsewhere, let’s return to our bell-shaped curve of where malaria thrives.
The study by Carlson and colleagues found results very similar to previous studies on the optimal conditions for malaria-carrying mosquitoes: transmission peaks at around 25°C.
In 1901, the average temperature in West Africa was around 26°C — very close to, but just past, the ideal temperature. 5 Climate change has increased temperatures, pushing them away from the optimum and down the slope.
What has happened elsewhere? East and Central Africa started below the optimum, at around 22°C, and Southern Africa far below, at around 17°C. Higher temperatures in all of these regions have pushed them closer to the optimum. East and Central Africa now sit at around 24°C, and Southern Africa at around 18°C.
It’s this temperature effect that has driven these diverging patterns across sub-Saharan Africa. The authors in the study did not find a clear signal from flooding or drought that has changed the historical distribution or prevalence of malaria, so far.
What’s crucial is that, while climate change has, on net, probably increased the burden of malaria across sub-Saharan Africa, its impact has been small compared with the many interventions and investments made to control and alleviate malaria. Malaria cases and deaths have not increased, but fallen substantially,

articles.title_orig: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
articles.title_zh: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
articles.content_orig:
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.
Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF fighters have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and allied groups and government forces in parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.
The presidents of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan - which all have strained relations with Ethiopia - met on Sunday in the Egyptian coastal city of El-Alamein.
They called for "respecting the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states" and the resolution of disputes through "peaceful means".
Ethiopia accuses Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan of supporting the Tigray rebels, which they deny.
Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.
Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.
Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.
The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.
Ethiopia and Egypt have been embroiled in a longer dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam built on the River Nile, which Cairo fears could reduce its share of water from the river.
On Sunday, the four leaders meeting in Egypt affirmed respect sovereignty and non-interference in the internal affairs of the regional states, while calling for adherence to international law over the usage of Nile waters.
In a joint statement, they rejected "unilateral measures" that could harm downstream countries, in an apparent reference to tensions over Ethiopia's dam.

articles.title_orig: People on the Move: World Bank, HSBC, J.P. Morgan, IA Global
articles.title_zh: People on the Move: World Bank, HSBC, J.P. Morgan, IA Global
articles.content_orig:
Home Banking People on the Move: World Bank, HSBC, J.P. Morgan, IA Global
Authors: Anthony Noto , Rob Daly
Major executive moves and leadership changes across the finance industry.
This article appears in the September 2026 issue of Global Finance Magazine.
The World Bank Group appointed Michael Kremer to be the organization’s chief economist and senior vice president for development economics.
Most recently, he served as director of the University of Chicago’s Development Innovation Lab, where he researched economic growth, technological change, and development economics. Kermer, Abhijit Banerjee, and Esther Duflo jointly won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2019 for their “experimental approach to alleviating global poverty.
Kremer “has spent his career not just identifying what works in development but proving it at scale,” said Ajay Banga, President of the World Bank Group. “That is exactly the kind of thinking we need.” —Rob Daly
After more than a decade at HSBC, Pam Kaur will step down as Group CFO , a position she has held since January 2025, before the bank’s 2027 annual meeting.
She will assume an advisory role to support Group CEO Georges Elherdy and ensure a smooth transition for her successor.
Kaur began her career in 2013 as group head of internal audit before advancing to the head of wholesale market and credit risk, group chief risk officer, group chief risk and compliance officer, and eventually group CFO.
Brendan Nelson, HSBC Group Holding plc chairman, praised Kaur for her “strong judgment and integrity.” She will leave the Group CFO role with the firm’s “deepest thanks and best wishes,” he added. —Rob Daly
J.P. Morgan named Nelle Miller and William Sinclair as co-CEOs of its U.S. Private Bank in September.
The pair leads the firm’s $2.4 trillion U.S. private banking business, overseeing more than 5,500 professionals across 57 offices who serve the wealthiest individuals, family offices, and institutions nationwide.
The appointments follow the July 2025 naming of David Frame as global CEO of J.P. Morgan Private Bank. Miller and Sinclair joined in 2002 and 2007, respectively. Miller currently heads the firm’s New York market, while Sinclair leads the Financial Leaders Group.
“We have a fantastic franchise, with exceptional people and an unparalleled breadth of capabilities,” Sinclair said. —Anthony Noto
IA Global Capital, a technology-focused investment bank with offices in New York and London, announced that Jules Wurlod has joined the firm as managing director.
Wurlod has served as M&A director for circular businesses at Houlihan Lokey since 2020, focusing on circular technology services such as device-as-a-service, IT asset management, IT asset disposition, recommerce, and trade-in. He previously worked as a project leader at Boston Consulting Group, advising Fortune 500 companies and government officials across Europe and the Middle East on corporate strategy and sustainability. —Anthony Noto

articles.title_orig: Long Beach child hospitalized with rare disease related to West Nile virus
articles.title_zh: Long Beach child hospitalized with rare disease related to West Nile virus
articles.content_orig:
The boy first developed rashes before showing worse symptoms. Charisse Gibson reports for the NBC4 News at 4 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026.
A Southern California boy faces a potentially lengthy recovery after being hospitalized with West Nile virus, prompting his mother to warn other parents about the early signs as Los Angeles County sees a record number of mosquito-borne infections.
As 13-year-old Joseph Vasquez remains unable to walk while being treated at Los Angeles Children's Hospital, his mother, Maria Salazar, told NBC Los Angeles that she was fearful her son could die.
Stream Los Angeles News for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
It all started with a rash that looked like chickenpox, according to Salazar. Then Joseph took a fall at school before developing other symptoms, including a fever, loss of appetite and headaches.
"We ended up taking him to the emergency room because I found him facedown on the ground," the mother said, explaining that Joseph had been losing his balance before he was diagnosed with West Nile virus. "It just started to be from the lower body, and then he couldn't even feel his toes or movement."
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that about 80% of West Nile virus infections are asymptomatic, while less than 1% of infected people develop neuroinvasive disease.
"Most of the cases, we have fever, maybe you just feel like funny," Dr. Ilan Shapiro of AltaMed Health Services said. "But there are cases, and that's why it's so important to talk about these viruses that can have problems, neurologically speaking, in our kids."
Shapiro, who is not Joseph's doctor, said inflammation caused by the infection may be making it challenging for the 13-year-old to walk.
"Our body is actually made of nerves and other things that actually connect our brain to our body. Sometimes that part of the connection can actually get inflamed, and that's where you can actually have this," the doctor explained.
Salazar, who initially thought her son had a common cold, now urges other parents to take proper precautions when kids go outdoors and pay attention to symptoms — the signs she initially brushed off.
"They should be looking out for any mosquito bites, dizziness, headaches, blurry vision, falling, losing balance," she said. "If your kids are telling you, 'Hey, my head hurts,' and they're scratching, take them to the doctor."
Dr. Shapiro said it's important to seek medical attention if people experience symptoms such as fever, chills, brain fog and fatigue, especially after spending time outdoors.
Los Angeles County has recorded 135 confirmed West Nile virus infections this year, including 130 hospitalizations and five deaths, according to the county Department of Public Health.

articles.title_orig: U.S. military removes bombers from U.K. base targeted in suspected terror plot
articles.title_zh: U.S. military removes bombers from U.K. base targeted in suspected terror plot
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England that is used by American military forces to strike Iran after an investigation discovered a planned terror attack, The Associated Press reported Sunday.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, AP reported, citing a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance and others have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war, AP said. These observers saw many B-1 bombers take off from the base on Sunday.
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, authorities took six individuals into custody and later released them on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the terror plot to Tehran, although Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford is located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London and has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
At least two vessels were struck over the weekend in waters near Oman and Iran , the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported, as Tehran reiterated its position on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen unless its conditions for ending the war with the U.S. are met.
On Saturday, the UKMTO, a British maritime security alert service, said it received a report of a crude oil tanker being hit by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman. It said another tanker was reported as being similarly struck Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room.
Attacks on shipping in the strait, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies moved before the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war on Feb. 28, have been happening on a regular basis for weeks.
"The Strait of Hormuz will not open until Iran's seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, and Iran will not regulate its national security with tweets from American officials," Iranian state media agency Nour News quoted Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying Sunday.
President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed an interim deal in June, known as the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, that resulted in a brief hiatus in fighting.
Tehran's conditions for allowing ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz include a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the U.S. naval blockade of its ports and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets.
A key demand of the U.S. has been that Iran dismantle its nuclear weapons program.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure reportedly came under renewed attacks.
Reuters reported Saturday that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had targeted a facility owned by Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco in the capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. The group said the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces.
A large plume of smoke and fire rose above the facility, Reuters quoted a witness as saying.
Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported attack. Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment.
If confirmed, it would be the latest escalation in what has effectively become a second front in the Iran war.
Some investors say they expect full-scale fighting to resume in the Middle East.
"The situation is fluid and volatile. To me, as we are developing and looking at the situation, it's not a question of if, but when the conflict resumes full force," Bader Al-Saif, founding president of Al-Saif Consulting, told CNBC's Access Middle East show on Friday.
The ongoing attacks and prospect of a further escalation have driven energy prices higher in recent weeks, raising inflation expectations globally and putting upward pressure on government borrowing costs .
Reports that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, pushed crude oil prices higher on Thursday. But prices edged lower Friday, after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease the burden on consumers.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, lost 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude shed $1.76 to settle at $91.11 per barrel.
— The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Saudi-Backed Yemen Forces Begin Bid to Retake Houthi Areas
articles.title_zh: Saudi-Backed Yemen Forces Begin Bid to Retake Houthi Areas
articles.content_orig:
The announcement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis reportedly cut a vital supply route to besieged city of Taiz
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis , even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia . The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title_orig: Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
articles.title_zh: Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
articles.content_orig:
Tens of thousands of people have rallied across Spain as protests have spread since the conservative-dominated parliament rejected a bill proposing measures to tackle a housing crisis.
Parliament on Friday voted down two decrees proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left-wing coalition government that were intended to address the housing crisis.
The protests erupted late last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home of 70 years in the capital, Madrid. Maria del Carmen Abascal’s eviction came after an international investment fund bought her building and hiked the rent.
Local media reports have suggested that Sanchez could call snap elections for as early as November after watching the strength of Saturday’s protests across the country. Spain’s current legislative term is set to end next summer.
Will the housing crisis trigger snap elections? Here’s what we know:
The emergency measures proposed by Spain’s leftist government to tackle the country’s housing affordability crisis failed to pass on Friday.
The government had proposed two measures to protect renters in the country. The first decree was meant to stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder, impose tighter restrictions on short-term leases and provide tax incentives to encourage renting and the construction of housing.
The second decree proposed making leases automatically renew when they are set to expire, essentially making them indefinite. A property owner would have to pay a tenant 12 months of rent to break the contract.
Sanchez, who leads a coalition government composed of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar, ⁠appealed to lawmakers in the run-up to the vote to put aside political calculations and pressure.
“Think about ordinary people, about those who most need the protection of public institutions. Think about the millions of young people who ⁠cannot afford to ⁠move out of their parents’ homes. Think about the families living with the constant ⁠anxiety of ever-rising rents,” he said before the voting.
But his government’s proposed measures were shot down by the majority of ⁠the 350-seat lower house of parliament.
The right-wing ⁠Catalan separatist ⁠party Junts refused to back the housing decrees, saying they would ultimately tighten the housing market. The centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox also voted against the measures.
Miriam Nogueras of Junts argued the decrees would lead only to owners removing their properties from the rental market and thus driving up prices even further.
“If they really wanted to protect people, collar the vulture funds, and reactivate housing, they would have already done it. They’ve had eight years,” she added on X, referring to Sanchez’s government.
Health Minister Monica Garcia said on X that the right-wing parties “have voted for a feudal economy in which a minority extracts the salary from a majority that works for their luxuries. And they do it against their own voters, who also suffer increasingly high rents, live in fear that the contract will end and can even be evicted.”
“Today the right has given rent-seeking a parliamentary majority that it doesn’t have on the street, but it’s going to pay for it sooner rather than later,” she added.
Before the parliamentary vote, Marta Soler Gallart, head of the Department of Sociology at the University of Barcelona, explained that neither of the two decrees addressed the housing problem in the medium or long term.
“Models such as Vienna’s with its low rents are cited in support of these decrees, but it is overlooked that the Vienna model and others have low rents because of their long history of creating and maintaining public social housing,” Soler Gallart told Al Jazeera on September 30.
“In Spain, however, public funds are invested in social housing which, after a while, the recipients sell at market price.”
Soler Gallart also said the new measures disadvantage landlords with small or few properties by extending five-year tenancy agreements by a further two years and by providing an indefinite extension of their leases.
“However, these extensions are not compulsory if the landlord can prove that they need the property for their own use,” she said.
Protests erupted across Spain in late September after 87-year-old Abascal was evicted from her home. The investment fund that bought her building hiked her rent by more than 200 percent to roughly $1,880 a month, a move aimed at pushing out the long-term tenant to make way for lucrative tourist apartments.
In recent years, Spain has seen protests against mass tourism, which has been linked to the housing crisis and soaring cost of living. Spain is the second most visited country in the world, attracting 97 million tourists last year.
While Abascal has returned to her home, according to her representatives, she has become the face of the country’s housing crisis, and people across Spain have been demanding the government address the issue.
Angered by parliament’s rejection of the government measures, tens of thousands of people took to the streets.
“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined Saturday’s protest in Madrid, told the Reuters news agency.
“It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
While the protests were mostly peaceful, in the southeastern city of Valencia, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up demonstrations. About 30 protesters managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building, before police removed them.
Meanwhile, in Madrid, Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group and fired rubber bullets on Saturday night.
Far-right activists, some of whom performed Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped out in the Puerta del Sol, a central square in the Spanish capital, the Spanish government said.
Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants’ Union, said Saturday’s rallies revealed “a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time and energy that is showing that eight days of people’s power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government”.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” Racu added.
Housing is a sensitive issue in Spain because it impacts how people vote. The average rent in the country has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square metre has risen from 8.20 euros (about $9.08 at the time) in 2016 to 15.1 euros ($17.15) this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.
In an October 1 article for Vanity Fair, Spanish journalist Jorge Dioni Lopez noted that after eight years in power, housing is what is causing Sanchez to lose support among educated young people, children of the middle classes.
“The government faces a difficult situation. Firstly, because most of the relevant powers lie with other levels of government. Secondly, because Spain is a nation of homeowners. Unlike in other European countries, almost all the public housing that has been built has ended up in private hands, and historically, homeownership has been more attractive than renting,” he wrote.
“Housing is our savings system and also the primary means of transmitting wealth between generations,” he added.
After Spain’s parliament rejected the government’s housing reform bills on Friday, the leader of the centre-right People’s Party, (PP) Alberto Nunez Feijoo, urged Sanchez to “call elections as soon as possible”, claiming he had the support of “neither the streets nor parliament”.
While Sanchez has not officially announced new elections, the Spanish online news site El Diario has reported that elections could take place as early as November 29. Spain’s general elections are currently scheduled for July 2027.

articles.title_orig: France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests
articles.title_zh: France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests
articles.content_orig:
Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said.
He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.
High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.
The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".
"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".
On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors.
Organisers of the protests have called for the demonstrations to continue on Tuesday after accusing the government of a lack of "concrete measures", according to AFP.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his government is taking further steps to "address the difficulties faced by high school students and educational staff".
He said this includes ensuring classes continue, improving facilities, better organising school days and making the French university admissions platform more transparent.
Lecornu also said the government is accelerating the review of its "vandal-pays" bill to ensure that people responsible for damage bear the cost of their actions.

articles.title_zh: Lotus Tech to Join WasabiCard's TOKEN2049 Singapore Side Event, Spotlighting Real-World Stablecoin Applications
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- WasabiCard, a stablecoin -powered global payment infrastructure platform, announced that it will host its TOKEN2049 Singapore Side Event, " STABLECOIN & PAYMENTS: FUNDS FLOW," on October 6 at Raffles Singapore.
Lotus Technology Inc. (Nasdaq: LOT) ("Lotus Tech"), a leading global intelligent and luxury mobility provider under globally renowned automotive brand Lotus, has confirmed its participation in the event. Dr. Daxue Wang, Chief Financial Officer of Lotus Tech, will join a featured panel discussion alongside senior representatives from Visa, Circle, Nium, Plume, Safeheron, OSL, WIDTH, AWS and other leading organizations across traditional finance, stablecoins and technology, exploring how stablecoins can move beyond on-chain settlement and become more deeply integrated into the real economy and everyday global payments.
From Stablecoin Settlement to Real-World Payments
As stablecoin infrastructure continues to mature, the industry's focus is expanding beyond the efficient movement of funds on-chain toward a broader question: how can stablecoin liquidity reach business operations, consumer payments and everyday commercial activity?
The event will focus on how funds move between on-chain financial systems and the real world, with two core discussions: "Wall Street On-Chain: The Next Era of Tokenized Capital Markets" and " Stablecoins Go Mainstream: From Settlement to Real-World Payments." Spanning capital markets and real-world payment scenarios, the discussions will explore what comes next as stablecoin adoption continues to scale.
For WasabiCard, bringing stablecoins into mainstream commercial use requires more than efficient on-chain settlement. It also requires infrastructure capable of connecting digital liquidity with card networks, local banking systems and payment scenarios across global markets.
"The next stage of stablecoin payments is not just about moving funds more efficiently on-chain, but about making those funds truly usable across business operations and consumers' everyday payment scenarios," said Ray Yang, Co-Founder and CEO of WasabiCard . "Having global brands like Lotus join the conversation is important because scaling stablecoin adoption requires stronger connections between payment infrastructure, real-world industries and commercial use cases. We also look forward to exploring further opportunities with Lotus."
Through its global card issuing and global remittance capabilities, WasabiCard helps businesses connect digital asset liquidity with real-world payments, providing more integrated infrastructure for moving and using funds across borders.
Lotus Brings a Global Automotive and Premium Consumer Perspective
With seven decades of boundary-pushing heritage and a legacy of motorsport championships, Lotus continues to redefine the limits of performance in racing and building the most engaging road cars in the world in the era of electrification and intelligence for global customers. As a truly global brand, Lotus boasts worldwide manufacturing footprints, leverages a global supply‑chain ecosystem, and maintains deep‑rooted business presence across multiple international markets. As the automotive industry becomes increasingly integrated with digital services and new consumer experiences, seamless global payment infrastructure is becoming an important bridge between brands and customers worldwide.
By welcoming Lotus to the event, WasabiCard aims to extend the stablecoin payment conversation beyond financial infrastructure and into real-world business and consumer scenarios.
During the event, Dr. Daxue Wang, CFO of Lotus Tech , will join the panel " Stablecoins Go Mainstream: From Settlement to Real-World Payments," exchanging perspectives with WasabiCard and other industry leaders on how stablecoins can connect global fund flows with real-world business needs, while sharing insights and experience from the global automotive and consumer sectors.
WasabiCard and Lotus to Explore Deeper Collaboration Opportunities
The TOKEN2049 Singapore Side Event will also provide an opportunity for WasabiCard and Lotus to deepen their engagement.
Building on their shared focus on global business and next-generation payment experiences, WasabiCard and Lotus are exploring opportunities for deeper collaboration across stablecoin payments, global payment infrastructure and real-world commercial scenarios.
Going forward, the two companies aim to combine Lotus' experience across global automotive and consumer scenarios with WasabiCard's capabilities in stablecoin payments and global payment infrastructure, exploring new ways to connect stablecoin technology with real-world commerce and consumer experiences.
About STABLECOIN & PAYMENTS: FUNDS FLOW
Hosted by WasabiCard, " STABLECOIN & PAYMENTS: FUNDS FLOW" will take place on October 6, 2026, at Raffles Singapore.
The event will bring together leading representatives across traditional finance, stablecoins , cross-border payments, digital assets and cloud computing for in-depth discussions on tokenized capital markets, real-world stablecoin payments and global fund flows.

WasabiCard powers payment use cases across media buying, SaaS subscriptions, global payroll, treasury management, and digital financial applications.

articles.title_orig: Here’s how Western Pa. school districts are preparing amid a statewide surge in measles cases
articles.title_zh: Here’s how Western Pa. school districts are preparing amid a statewide surge in measles cases
articles.content_orig:
Most counties don’t have their own health agencies, and some specific population groups have low vaccination rates
Pennsylvania is bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials concerned that it’s “only a matter of time” until the disease spreads beyond the outbreak’s epicenter.
Last week the state reported its fifth measles-associated death amid 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. The outbreak comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by increasing vaccine skepticism, especially due to the power and influence of controversial health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr .
Contributing to the challenge is that Pennsylvania is one of the few US states where its counties mostly lack their own health department, with only seven of its 67 counties having their own.
Lancaster county, which doesn’t have its own health department, has seen the highest amount of cases, at 381, believed to be mostly among the Amish or similar religious groups who have historically low rates of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine uptake. Health officials, doctors and other members of the community in the county are now attempting to establish its own health department to better tackle the outbreak.
Jeanne Franklin , the director of Chester county’s health department, said that her county, which has the third highest number of cases, at 83, is preparing for an influx of cases from neighboring Lancaster.
“We have a very long border with Lancaster county, and these types of disease don’t care about borders,” Franklin said. “It’s going to keep going and find a person who isn’t vaccinated. We’re operating with the assumption that the disease may jump and spread to non-Plain [Amish] community members. Our goal is to prevent that, but we assume that it may happen.”
She added that although many Amish people have not been vaccinated, it’s not because they are anti-vaxxers, but rather because “they were either unaware of it or they don’t seek out healthcare as frequently as other residents”.
She added: “But they’re willing to have the conversation and make a decision on what’s happening today. They’re not making decisions based on the myths out there, but because their neighbors are impacted.”
Amid active surveillance of measles cases, contact tracing and setting up community vaccination centers, the county is also working to dispel misinformation some of its residents have regarding the safety of the vaccine.
“We have people in key positions saying it isn’t an outbreak, it isn’t a problem. We have people who approach our nurses and say that they were told the vaccine will make them sterile, or that there’s a microchip within it,” Franklin said.
But for Franklin, the fact that Chester county is one of the few counties to have its own health department is a clear advantage in the race to stop the spread of the disease.
“By having our own health department [it] means that we already have the infrastructure in place, and we prepare for these things all year round,” Franklin said. “With the number of counties [the state has] to provide support to, they can’t possibly know all the key partners in a geographical area.”
She added: “The state has a finite set of employees, while I can pull my employees away from their normal jobs and say we need help with this. We live here, we know it, and we’re working with the communities and the organizations who know us. I think every county needs a health department, but we’re just not set up that way in Pennsylvania while other states are.”
Dr Richard Lorraine, the medical director of Montgomery county’s office of public health, said that it is a “matter of time” before the third most populous county in Pennsylvania will begin to see measles cases.
“We recognize that essentially it’s all around us, and so a big focus for the county is immunization,” Lorraine said. “It’s the best preventative measure and where the county is focusing its efforts on.”
after newsletter promotion
Working closely with community organizers, Lorraine said the county was making sure that every resident was able to be vaccinated regardless of their insurance status.
“Because we are a public health agency, our mandate is to provide for members of our population for the most part who are underinsured, and there’s a very high percentage who aren’t insured,” Lorraine said. “And through our partnership with pharmacies we’re able to open these clinics for everyone. So whether you have insurance or if you don’t, we can work it out so that someone is able to administer a vaccine.”
Lora Werner, the director of the Delaware county health department, said that her agency is facing several challenges in protecting residents from the virus.
Among them was the collapse of Crozer Health, Delaware county’s largest healthcare system, due to bankruptcy last year.
“They were a huge provider of pediatric care,” Werner said. “And although we do have a high vaccination rate across Delaware county, there are pockets where they aren’t as good.”
For Werner, the newly established local health department has been a gamechanger for promoting public health initiatives in the county.
“We are the newest health department on the block, and we’re so passionate about the fact that we’re now here and can serve our residents,” Werner said. “We’re deeply integrated into the social networks.”
She added: “Creating a new department was very challenging, and we’re a very odd state in this regard,” Werner said. “If you want to have one you need to have a referendum to establish one. But it’s not required, so we have a mishmash of the counties that have taken that step and those that have not.”
The Guardian has approached the Pennsylvania health department for comment.

articles.title_orig: Morning Bid: The euro has a France problem
articles.title_zh: Morning Bid: The euro has a France problem
articles.content_orig:
France’s Cac 40 index slides as announcement of snap election in Spain also helps fuel eurozone uncertainty
Business live – latest updates
The euro has slumped to the lowest level against the dollar in 17 months amid growing concern France’s debt position could threaten the stability of the wider single currency bloc.
The single currency fell as much as 0.8% against the dollar in early trading on Monday to below $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025, before recovering slightly. It has slumped by about 1.2% this month, accelerating a drop of about eight cents against the greenback from a peak of $1.20 in January.
Investors said the sell-off in the euro was fuelled by concerns over France’s rising debt costs as the government battles to control its stretched public finances in the run-up to next year’s presidential election.
France’s blue-chip Cac 40 index of leading company shares fell by 1% on Monday, as markets elsewhere across Europe rallied. The FTSE 100 was up 0.2%, while Germany’s Dax was little changed.
Monday’s announcement of a snap election in Spain by the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency housing legislation last week has also fuelled eurozone uncertainty. Madrid’s benchmark Ibex 35 index rose by 0.5%.
“Europe is taking the spotlight at the start of the week, as fiscal and political concerns hit the bloc,” said Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB. “France is the epicentre of the concerns; however, Spain is also set to get ready for an early election, which is adding to investor worries.”
Amid a global sell-off in sovereign debt as the Iran war rattles markets, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on French 10-year government bonds last week hit the highest level since 2002, before dipping back on Friday.
This pushed the gap between France and Germany’s borrowing costs, an important measure of investor concern, to its widest level since 2012 at the height of the eurozone sovereign debt crisis .
Investors are focused on Paris’s fiscal position and concerns that the presidential election and a hung parliament – with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party gaining ground – could make it tougher for the government to curtail a yawning budget deficit.
The minority government of the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, announced plans last month for a €54bn (£45.8bn) savings drive to curb borrowing levels, setting the stage for a fierce political battle.
With President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration under pressure amid strikes and protests across the country , the budget measures involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence.
Lecornu said the savings would result in limiting a budget deficit of 5.5% of GDP this year to 5% next year. He warned that without action the shortfall between public spending and revenue could reach 6.5%.
after newsletter promotion
However, investors fear political pressures could derail fiscal consolidation, threatening to push up borrowing and adding to France’s debt pile at a time of soaring government borrowing costs.
Analysts warned the stresses in the French bond market could spread to other countries in the euro area, stoking fears over a return to the dynamics of the 2010s sovereign debt crisis.
It comes amid concerns over the test facing the European Central Bank from mounting inflationary pressures from the war in the Middle East and the risk France’s debt problem spreads throughout the euro area.
Roberto Mialich, a currency strategist at the Italian bank UniCredit, said: “Investors still do not rule out riding a further decline of the euro, making a retest of $1.10 possible in the near term.
“This is also because growing political tensions across the eurozone (primarily in France and Spain) and fears of contagion across the European sovereign debt market are putting pressure on the euro.”

articles.title_orig: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.title_zh: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has continued rallying for Republican candidates while visiting Ohio, proposing a defiant outlook on his party’s chances in the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump told a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, that he believes there will be a “big surprise” in the upcoming elections, claiming his Democratic opponents do not know what is happening.
Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, but the US president said Republicans would do better than critics expect.
“Just get out and vote,” Trump said as he rallied for US Senator Jon Husted, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and other Republicans.
“If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big,” he said.
Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds, with Trump’s popularity falling in recent months as higher petrol prices and those for other staples persist amid the US-Israel war ⁠⁠on Iran.
Husted, a Republican in a competitive Ohio race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, hopes the president can motivate supporters who might otherwise skip midterm elections.
Trump garnered more than 55 percent of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings.
Ohio petrol prices increased 35 percent over the past year to $4.16 per gallon (3.8 litres) on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which compiles data ⁠⁠on automobile travel. Trump’s trade policy with Canada has also led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3bn worth of Ohio exports, based ⁠⁠on 2025 figures, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported.
Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday’s rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war “on our terms” and, in the interim, he is “showing people that I’m fighting for lower prices”.
Trump extensively promoted his administration’s action on data centres, mainly those built for AI, during the rally, saying he was seeking to ensure they “benefit local communities” and praising Husted for an unsuccessful attempt to push forward legislation on the issue.
“Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” he said, repeating his defence of data centres.
Data centres have become a hot political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies.
The issue became especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centres to the Midwestern state as lieutenant governor.
The Republican-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats.
“Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centres in Ohio,” Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump’s visit. “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

articles.title_orig: US criticism of Starbucks in Xinjiang rejected
articles.title_zh: US criticism of Starbucks in Xinjiang rejected
articles.content_orig:
China has firmly rejected criticism from a US congressional committee regarding Starbucks' expansion into the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. Beijing stressed that the move of the US consumer giant demonstrates the region's social stability and economic vitality as more domestic and international brands tap its growing consumer market.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Saturday that claims of so-called genocide in Xinjiang are "a blatant lie", in response to a question about criticism from the US House Select Committee on China, which had described Starbucks' decision to open stores in the region as "morally bankrupt".
"Relevant US institutions are accustomed to fabricating issues and attacking and smearing China for political purposes, and have no credibility whatsoever," Guo said.
READ MORE: US blacklisting slammed as destructive bullying
"Xinjiang today enjoys social stability, economic development, ethnic unity and religious harmony," he added. "China will continue to expand high-standard opening-up and provide more opportunities for foreign companies to invest and operate in China."
Starbucks opened its first two stores in Xinjiang on Sept 29, both in Urumqi, the regional capital — one at the city's Grand Bazaar and the other at Urumqi Tianshan International Airport. The openings marked the global coffee chain's debut in the region and its latest expansion in China, its second-largest market after the US.
The Grand Bazaar flagship store incorporates local elements into its design, including Atlas silk, ethnic musical instruments and bazaar-inspired architecture.
The airport outlet adopts a "silk road station" concept to serve travelers at the regional transport hub. Both locations feature locally inspired offerings.
During the weeklong National Day holiday, a Xinjiang-inspired drink and three food items are also being offered at more than 2,700 Starbucks stores across 41 Chinese cities, bringing the region's flavors to consumers nationwide.
"Entering Xinjiang is not only about further expanding our store network, but also gives us an opportunity to go deeper into this vibrant market and build long-term connections with consumers here," said Molly Liu, CEO of Starbucks China, adding that the company would continue to deepen its presence in Xinjiang and develop stores, products and experiences tailored to local demand.
Starbucks is not alone in looking to the region for growth. Domestic giant Luckin Coffee opened its first 11 self-operated stores in Urumqi in May 2024, while Cotti Coffee had entered the Xinjiang market earlier through its franchise model.
The expansion of major coffee brands comes alongside strong growth in Xinjiang's tourism sector. The region received 323 million tourist visits in 2025, up 8 percent year-on-year, with tourism spending rising 8.4 percent in the same period to 370 billion yuan ($52 billion), according to regional government data.
ALSO READ: Services seen having bigger role in GDP
Retail sales have also returned to growth this year. Xinjiang's retail sales of consumer goods reached 263.03 billion yuan in the first eight months of 2026, up 0.3 percent year-on-year, after declining 0.3 percent in the first seven months, official data showed.
The region's broader corporate base is also expanding. Xinjiang had 2,647 registered foreign-invested enterprises by the end of June, up 6.91 percent from a year earlier, while the total number of registered market entities reached 2.73 million, according to regional market regulators.
Nationwide, China saw 35,000 newly established foreign-invested enterprises in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year-on-year, according to the State Administration for Market Regulation. The number of newly established foreign-invested enterprises in wholesale and retail rose 11.9 percent.

articles.title_orig: UK Weighs Higher Tariffs on Chinese EVs Under EU Pressure
articles.title_zh: UK Weighs Higher Tariffs on Chinese EVs Under EU Pressure
articles.content_orig:
Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures
Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe , as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely , and the EU imposes duties of up to 45% .
EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.
Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China .
Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models , and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant , from investing further in the UK.
“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.
“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”
Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.
Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.
Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.
The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.
Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”
after newsletter promotion
Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”
He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”
Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.
Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.
Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.
Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”
He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

articles.title_orig: Russia hospitalizes almost 200 people after researcher's death from plague: Reports
articles.title_zh: Russia hospitalizes almost 200 people after researcher's death from plague: Reports
articles.content_orig:
Nearly 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Russia's Irkutsk region in eastern Siberia over suspected exposure to plague, according to local media reports.
The report said 189 people were being monitored following the illness of an employee at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk. Alexei Tsydenov, head of the nearby Republic of Buryatia, said the woman had died from an unspecified form of plague.
Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday that the employee had been diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov remained stable.
The agency said expanded testing had not detected microorganisms linked to the employee's work.
The update follows local media reports on Friday that a 27-year-old employee at an anti-plague institute had fallen ill with suspected pneumonic plague after returning from a work trip to Buryatia, where an outbreak had been reported near the border with Mongolia, citing Russian Telegram channel Mash.
The White House is monitoring reports of the suspected case and related quarantines in Russia, Axios reported Sunday, citing a Trump administration official. The official said the administration was "aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options," the report said.
The Russian and Moscow ministries of health, the World Health Organization and the U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
