articles.title_orig: Tens of thousands protest against Spain's housing crisis following eviction of 87-year-old woman
articles.title_zh: Tens of thousands protest against Spain's housing crisis following eviction of 87-year-old woman
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle ⁠a mounting housing crisis ⁠after ​government measures were struck down by the opposition.
Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike ⁠after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in ⁠Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on ​Friday.
Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000.
“It’s a shame,” Nando ‌de Anguulo, 26, ‌who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it ‌is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the ‌legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s ​protests before making a decision.
The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta .
Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas ⁠to break up the protests.
About 30 people managed to get inside ​the City ​of Arts and Sciences, a ​landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ​ousted by ‌police.
One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian, 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital.
He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all, as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”.
Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room.”
“What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said.
after newsletter promotion
Late on Saturday groups of far-right protesters, some of them performing Nazi salutes, tried to get to the camp in Madrid but were blocked by police.
One video posted on the website of Spanish daily El País showed police chasing some members of the group through the streets and the newspaper also reported that officers had made three arrests.
On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.
The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.
News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.
The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years . The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China's railway passenger trips hit record single-day high
articles.title_zh: China's railway passenger trips hit record single-day high
articles.content_orig:
Passengers line up at the boarding gates at Shenzhen North Railway Station in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, October 1, 2026. /VCG
China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on October 1, the first day of the week-long National Day holiday, setting a new single-day record, China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said Friday.
On October 2, the railway network is expected to handle 20.39 million passenger trips, with 1,462 additional trains scheduled to meet the high demand, the company said.
Passenger ticket pre-sales show that the most popular departure cities on Friday include Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Nanjing, while popular arrival cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Nanjing and Changsha.
Routes such as Xi'an-Chengdu round trips, as well as those from Beijing to Shenyang, Zhengzhou and Qingdao are among the busiest.
Railway authorities across the country have strengthened transport organization and implemented measures to ensure safe, convenient and comfortable travel.
China Railway Taiyuan Group has coordinated with local transport departments and scenic spots to add shuttle buses linking Datong South Station with the Yungang Grottoes, a UNESCO World Heritage site featuring more than 50,000 Buddhist stone sculptures, and the Hengshan Mountain scenic area in north China's Shanxi Province.
China Railway Hohhot Group has added 11 multiple-unit trains to the Baotou-Wuhai section of the Baotou-Yinchuan high-speed railway.
China Railway Wuhan Group, tapping the newly opened Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, has launched a promotion campaign with local governments in Yichang and Xingshan, offering passengers exclusive discounts at scenic spots, hotels and homestays when they present their train tickets.
China Railway expects some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which runs from September 23 to October 8.

articles.title_orig: Government forces seize capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region from rebels
articles.title_zh: Government forces seize capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region from rebels
articles.content_orig:
By Deborah Castellano Lubov
"Above all, the Ethiopian Catholic Church earnestly calls upon all parties to open their hearts to forgiveness and reconciliation by renewing the spirit of brotherhood and sisterhood among us, so that our nation may experience a just, lasting, and authentic peace."
This was the appeal emphasized by the Catholic Bishops of Ethiopia in a letter issued by the Catholic Bishopsâ Conference of Ethiopia (CBCE) on Thursday.
The message began by stressing that the Ethiopian Catholic Church grieves deeply over the armed conflict currently present in Tigray, Afar, Amhara, Oromia, and other regions of the country.
"Rather than resolving differences," the Bishops said, "war serves only to deepen divisions and multiplies suffering. It claims a tragic toll on precious human lives, inflicts grave devastation upon communities and property, and sows seeds of hatred, resentment, and vengeance that may endure for generations."
The African Bishops echoed Pope Leo's appeal for peace at his Wednesday General Audience, after his return from his Apostolic Journey to France, where he said he was following with deep concern the situation in Tigray and in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, where hostilities have once again broken out.
"I extend," the Holy Father said, "my heartfelt plea to all parties to choose the path of dialogue. Armed conflict never solves problems but only worsens them, leaving in its wake a trail of death, destruction, and resentment. Only honest engagement can lay the foundations for lasting peace."
In continuity with the Holy Father's exhortation, the nation's Catholic Bishops appealed in their statement "to regard the life of others as we regard our own life and the suffering of others as our own suffering, because the peace of our beloved nation, Ethiopia, is a responsibility shared by all of us."
"It is our heartfelt prayer," they wrote, "that all disputes may be settled through genuine dialogue and that all forms of conflict may cease."
In a special way, they recalled the "painful" reality that whenever violence erupts, the greatest suffering falls upon the most vulnerable, particularly innocent people, children, women, the elderly, and the sick.
"We continue to raise our voice," the bishops said, "so that this may not happen and to implore the Lord to protect every human life. We therefore affirm that a peace rooted in truth, justice, forgiveness, and reconciliation can bring healing to our nation and serve the welfare of all our peoples. Such a peace reflects the values of the Gospel, advances the common good, upholds the sacred dignity of the human person, and corresponds to the will of God for His people."
The Bishops urged all Catholic faithful and all people of good will to persevere in prayer and fasting, imploring Almighty God to bestow upon their nation the blessings of reconciliation, unity, and lasting peace.

articles.title_orig: ‘Adua’ Collaboration Is Born From a Flower Between Worlds
articles.title_zh: ‘Adua’ Collaboration Is Born From a Flower Between Worlds
articles.content_orig:
Artwork by Karen Paulina Biswell & Maria Amilbia Siagama Siagama
Words by Karen Paulina Biswell
My collaboration with María Amilbia Siagama Siagama began 15 years ago, when I met her daughter in the streets of Bogotá, and continued into the mountains of Risaralda. It has been driven by curiosity, the desire to know one another, and learning to accept the opacity and misunderstandings that run through our relationship.
Our joint project, ADUA , takes its title from the Embera word for “I don’t know”—an embrace of uncertainty that offers a form of kinship that doesn’t erase difference, but learns to live with and through it. It also makes space for what does not need to be translated or explained.
My conversations with María Amilbia led me to the Benakúa ceremony, where men of knowledge drink a preparation made from the Brugmansia flower and travel to the underworld. For the Emberá, getting drunk and dreaming are intertwined: seeing and dreaming can become the same experience. What interested me was this idea of “knowing through forgetting.” What would it mean to forget the ways we had learned to see Indigenous communities? For me, it meant forgetting myself, opening myself to others, and allowing dreaming to become a way of seeing.
At the heart of ADUA is the Brugmansia, or iguaka, a sacred plant understood by the Emberá Chamí as a spiritual master and companion species. Its downward-facing flowers are associated with the world beneath us, a realm of knowledge and wisdom. In the Benakúa ceremony, the journey to this underworld can bring back guidance for tending the territory.
In these images, the Brugmansia becomes a kind of satellite between worlds—between seeing and dreaming, knowing and forgetting, memory and belief. It is through the flower that ADUA asks how we might encounter one another without needing to make everything fully known.

articles.title_orig: Florida weighs ditching property taxes and sticking Canadians with the bill
articles.title_zh: Florida weighs ditching property taxes and sticking Canadians with the bill
articles.content_orig:
Florida voters are weighing whether to scrap residential property taxes, and the state's governor has a solution to that potentially huge revenue loss: tax Canadians more.
Canadians who own property in Florida describe the threats to shake them down for more money as just the latest insult in a series of them since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power last year with a decidedly anti-Canada agenda.
Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has railed against property taxes, which fund local governments and the services they provide — law enforcement, fire, EMS, disaster preparation and mosquito control, among many others — equating them to a form of modern-day feudalism where homeowners must "pony up money to the government just for the courtesy of using your own property."
To end this, DeSantis is pushing Amendment 3, a ballot measure crafted by his Republican statehouse allies that will be put to voters in the midterm election next month.
If passed, Florida "homesteaders," as permanent residents are called, will see a dramatic increase in an existing property tax exemption.
Any Floridian with a primary residence valued at $250,000 US or less — about 60 per cent of all homesteaders, according to the governor's office, although that figure has been questioned — would pay nothing, and those with a home worth more than that would pay much less than they do now. The measure also calls on the state to eliminate homesteader property taxes entirely over time.
This constitutional amendment requires a 60 per cent supermajority, and at least one recent poll suggests it will easily clear that hurdle .
State economists project such a move will cost about $12 billion US annually , forcing local and county governments that depend on these taxes to make deep cuts, find new revenue elsewhere or both.
That's where things could get more expensive for the Canadians who own an estimated $60 billion US worth of property in the Sunshine State. DeSantis has explicitly described them as a resource to tap to close expected budget gaps.
"We need to focus on our Florida residents. And focus on, in this case, Florida homeowners, particularly our homesteaded homeowners, and we need to focus the relief there," DeSantis said at a news conference last year defending his call for lower property taxes instead of a sales tax cut.
"I want Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists subsidizing the state and making it so Florida residents pay less taxes. I don't want to give Canadians a tax cut."
In an interview with Fox Business in June, DeSantis said that while homesteader property tax revenue will be a fraction of what it once was if the measure passes, Canadian property owners won't see any of that relief, which could help pad local coffers.
"They tax property that is non-homestead: residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial. That's a lot of money that they have," DeSantis said of local and county governments.
While reducing taxes for Floridians, the ballot measure also dictates that the assessed value of a non-homesteaded property — owned by a Canadian or another non-resident — can increase by up to five per cent a year, steadily raising the revenue local governments can collect.
"They are going to start getting more revenue from existing taxes without having to add new taxes, and they're going to end up in a very stable situation very shortly," DeSantis said.
DeSantis has routinely poked at Canada — including its perennially losing hockey teams. He initially mocked the trade war-induced travel boycott, saying he didn't think it would meaningfully materialize, only to see his state tourism bureau report a double-digit drop in Canadian arrivals last year.
Some Canadians who have put down seasonal roots in the state have had enough of the taunts.
Glenn McGill of Wiarton, Ont., has been wintering in North Fort Myers, Fla., a community once well populated with fellow Canadian sunseekers, for the last 15 years.
But after Trump's second win, there's been what he describes as a "stampede" of Canadians out of the park he and his wife Deb long thought of as a second home.
He says there are only four Canadians left in the sprawling retirement community, a fraction of what there once was when he first started going south.
Some snowbirds want out of Florida. A bad housing market makes it hard to leave
McGill said DeSantis's threat to lean on Canadians to make up for lost property tax revenue will only drive more of them away, including himself — he listed his home for sale.
"They're a greedy bunch of SOBs," McGill said in an interview with CBC News. "They want to drive Canadians out."
"Those who are well off really don't care, but we're not rich, we're not broke, we can do the Florida thing comfortably, but starting to pay extra taxes — that would hurt," he said.
"And this political thing with Trump, I've had enough of it."
With so many Canadians leaving or staying away, McGill says the housing market in Florida has been tough to navigate as a seller.
"The market's pretty dry," he said. "It's listed, but it hasn't sold yet."
Canadians make up the vast majority of foreign property buyers in areas along Florida's Gulf Coast.
According to Realtor.com data, Canadians represent more than 70 per cent of international demand in the Cape Coral metropolitan area, which includes McGill's community.
And with Canadian sales nowhere near pre-trade war levels , the firm says local sellers face " real pricing pressure ," with properties listed for weeks longer than the national average .
The areas of Florida that have historically attracted the most Canadian interest are projected to see the largest drop in home prices this year, according to the firm's projections.
Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on 3, a group opposing the property tax ballot measure, anticipates more housing market shocks given a possible flood of new Canadian-owned home listings if this tax change takes effect.
"Gosh, it wouldn't surprise me if there's an exodus of Canadians — they are going to be hit significantly," Ousley said in an interview.
"Amendment 3 is a train wreck. It's a train wreck for Floridians. It's a train wreck for those who come in the winter. Those Canadian snowbirds are going to be impacted with additional taxes — this is a tax shift, it's not tax relief," she said.
Ousley said a shrinking Canadian population base alone can't replace what will be lost if homestead taxes disappear.
Many municipalities are already warning that a sudden erosion in their tax base will decimate public services, most notably law enforcement and 911 response times.
"Everyone is going to lose with cuts," she said.
John May of Ottawa offloaded his Key West, Fla., condo after getting sick of hearing people he thought were friends parrot Trump's harsh rhetoric about Canada.
He said he felt like he was swimming in "a sea of stupidity," with falsehoods about his country commonplace.
"Trump would say something stupid, Governor Trudeau, 51st state and all that, and they'd stand there and laugh and I'd say to myself, 'Well, I just lost all respect for you,'" May said in an interview.
"And then you start avoiding people because you know what the conversation is going to be. If you try and have a logical discussion with somebody who's a Trumper, just forget about it."
Jo-Ann Rowe, a Canadian who was wintering in Fort Lauderdale for years with no issue before Trump's return, had the same experience.
"The 51st state thing, my American friends all thought that was quite funny. And I really don't," she said.
She left Florida for a rental property in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. "I found it totally disrespectful. And I just couldn't do it anymore, this was my little part to do," she said.

articles.title_orig: Report says heat, fires left a third of the world living with 'extremely poor' air quality
articles.title_zh: Report says heat, fires left a third of the world living with 'extremely poor' air quality
articles.content_orig:
A European Union analysis released on Sept. 30 suggests that adding heat waves and wildfire smoke to existing air pollution has exposed about a third of the world's population to what it classified as "extremely poor" air quality.
Malay Mail reported that the European Union's Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service said 34% of people worldwide faced what it labeled "extremely poor" air quality from Jan. 1 through Sept. 15.
Another 17% of the global population fell into the "very poor" category, and only 5% reached what it described as "good" ozone levels.
Asia was hit the hardest, with 53% of the region's population in the "extremely poor" category and another 22% in "very poor" ozone conditions.
Those exposure categories were measured against World Health Organization guidance that caps eight-hour ozone exposure at 100 micrograms per cubic meter.
On hot, sunny days, pollution from vehicles, industry, and wildfires can react in the air to create ground-level ozone, a pollutant that can turn already polluted conditions into a major health risk.
Health effects can include damaged lung tissue, trouble breathing, and asthma attacks.
According to the analysis, record heatwaves and wildfires in Europe and North America helped drive the increase, with smoke spreading far beyond the burned areas.
Ozone has been especially hard to bring down, even as some other harmful pollutants have declined, because climate conditions make it easier to form. The analysis also pointed to major wildfires in Indonesia and said El Niño, which began in June, could contribute to more fires in Southeast Asia.
The Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service tracks pollution and wildfire activity using satellite data and computer models.
That helps explain why ozone remains a stubborn problem even after declines in some other major air pollutants over recent decades.
Dangerous air is not always local or visible. A stretch of hot, sunny weather combined with smoke or urban pollution can worsen air quality even far from a wildfire, making air-quality alerts more important during heat events.
As CAMS director Laurence Rouil said in the Atmosphere Watch report: "Air pollution does not stop at borders. It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans and affecting air quality far from its source."
These stories look at the same ozone and smoke threats highlighted in this report.
• Across the U.S., blazing heat and wildfires are wiping out air quality gains .
• Across the U.S., wildfire-driven ozone is linked to premature deaths far from the flames.
• In China, scientists found that winter ozone pollution can spike even without summer heat.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest oat milk producer joins climate journalism campaign
articles.title_zh: World’s largest oat milk producer joins climate journalism campaign
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK -- Oatly, the world's largest producer of oat milk, is sending a new message to its consumers: Most people want their governments to take action on climate change.
Splashed on the side of the Swedish company's cartons is messaging from the "89 Percent Project," a campaign launched by Covering Climate Now, a global journalism nonprofit.
Newsrooms traditionally try not to associate with organized advocacy efforts, but the unorthodox campaign has been gaining traction. Participating news organizations have amplified research that 80% to 89% of people worldwide want their governments to confront climate change.
Oatly's new cartons were first released in Sweden and have since been rolled out to other European nations, including Belgium and Germany. The cartons are expected to be on U.S. shelves by January, said Caroline Reid, senior sustainability director at Oatly.
"Companies should be taking much more responsibility, not only in reducing their own environmental footprint, but really working out how they can use their platform to drive a positive future," Reid said at an event last month during New York Climate Week.
In addition to producing stories on climate change, Covering Climate Now promotes reporting on the issue through journalism trainings, newsroom collaborations and press awards. It launched the "89 Percent Project" last year and describes it as a global collaborative journalism initiative.
The project takes its name from a 2024 study in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Nature Climate Change. Based on a survey of nearly 130,000 people across 125 countries, the study found that 89% of people want intensified political action on climate change.
Most people who want climate action don't realize they are in the "silent majority," said Mark Hertsgaard, executive director of Covering Climate Now. But that is beginning to change, as "elements of civil society all around the world pick up this 89% message and spread it themselves."
The project launched with several media partners, including The Guardian, Agence France-Presse and El País. In April, Japanese TV stations said over the next two years they would air announcements about how the majority of Japanese people want stronger climate action. In June, in a separate initiative, 136 Japanese news outlets also began spreading this messaging via social media platforms, news releases, and other forms of public communication.
Numerous polls, surveys and scientific studies in the U.S. have long found that a majority want the government to take more action on climate change, even if the issue is rarely brought up in political campaigns.
In a 2022 poll, The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that nearly two-thirds of Americans thought the federal government was not doing enough to fight climate change, which is primarily caused by the release of greenhouse gases when coal, oil and gas are burned.
That same year, a study based on responses from more than 6,000 Americans and published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Nature Communications found that most Americans underestimate the prevalence of support for major climate change mitigation policies and climate concern. While 66% to 80% of Americans support these policies, Americans think only 37% to 43% do.
"We felt that we, and our fellow journalists, were really missing the story here," said Hertsgaard, adding he believed the industry was inadvertently "misrepresenting a big part of the climate story, which is that most people around the world want this tackled."
Oatly's milk carton campaign is subtle, especially when compared to the more well-known 1980s U.S. milk carton campaign that put photos of missing children on cartons to spread awareness about their cases.
The new cartons feature two stacked text boxes on one side of the carton.
The much smaller top box reads: "Politicians! These eleven words represent people not interested in climate action." The lower box, which takes up most of the carton's side, has an 89-word message that makes the case that most people want their governments to take climate action and that doing so could lead to political wins.
Reid, with Oatly, first read about the climate project in The Guardian. As a company selling alternatives to cow milk, she said the project "aligns with what we're trying to do. We're trying to engage people and make them want to do something different."
Every organization, political party and brand can play a bigger role in contributing to societal net zero, meaning as much carbon being absorbed as is released into the atmosphere, and driving the transition to renewable energy, Reid said.
President Donald Trump has periodically railed about climate change and policies meant to address it, including transitioning to carbon-free energy like wind and solar. During the 2025 U.N. General Assembly, Trump called climate change a "con job" and renewable energy the "Green Scam."
This narrative, which goes against years of science that has established that human-caused emissions are driving the climate to change, has pushed some organizations to take a stronger stand in rebutting the administration and go a step further to advocate for solutions.
Covering Climate Now's project straddles a tightrope between advocacy and journalism, which experts say has pros and cons.
"The economic failures of so many news outlets have led to a rise in independent journalism that operates outside the norms established by legacy media outlets," said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation. "There is plenty of room for advocacy in journalism."
Clay Calvert, who specializes in First Amendment and freedom of expression issues at the University of Florida, said two dangers arise when journalism organizations partner with companies.
The first is that the journalism group will pull its punches and self-censor negative information about the corporate partner. The second is that the journalism organization will favorably portray its corporate partner in news coverage.
"There really needs to be a wall of separation in any newsroom between the interests of the journalism entity, including its readers and viewers, and those of its corporate partners," Calvert said. "Sometimes creating and maintaining that separation is easier said than done."
No money has changed hands between Covering Climate Now and Oatly, according to Hertsgaard, who called the company an "ally."
"As a journalist, I feel like we have to have the courage to not just report the facts, but to draw the connections," Hertsgaard said. "Now, if that amounts to advocacy, then that's an advocacy I'm comfortable with."
Information for this article was contributed by Jennifer McDermott of The Associated Press.

articles.title_orig: US Department of Justice indicts CEO for smuggling ‘AI chips’ into China
articles.title_zh: US Department of Justice indicts CEO for smuggling ‘AI chips’ into China
articles.content_orig:
A California technology entrepreneur accused of helping move more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers to China is at the center of one of the largest recent U.S. cases involving advanced artificial intelligence hardware and export restrictions.
Federal authorities arrested Greg Lui, 38, on Thursday, alleging he orchestrated a scheme to send high-end computer servers containing advanced U.S.-made graphics processing units, or GPUs, to China through third countries in violation of federal export-control laws.
Lui, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, faces charges of conspiracy to violate export-control regulations, smuggling, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. If convicted on all counts, he could face up to 50 years in prison.
According to federal prosecutors, Lui owns Earthmade Computer Inc., a technology company based in the City of Industry in Los Angeles County.
Public business profiles show Earthmade was founded in 2021 and operated in areas including server procurement, technology infrastructure, and data-center services.
According to public profiles, Lui's technology career began with work in hosting and colocation services before he launched Earthmade Computer. The company marketed itself as a provider of server procurement, infrastructure, and data-center solutions, placing it in the fast-growing market for advanced computing hardware during the boom in artificial intelligence investment.
Before entering the technology sector, Lui was involved in the restaurant business. Public profiles indicate he helped launch a San Gabriel Valley restaurant specializing in Sichuan cuisine before later transitioning into technology and data-center operations.
Authorities allege Earthmade became the vehicle through which export-controlled AI hardware was purchased and routed overseas.
The Justice Department said Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia -based shipping companies between January and October 2024 as part of the alleged operation.
Newsweek has reached out to Earthmade via email for comment after regular business hours.
According to the indictment, Lui and his co-conspirators acquired export-controlled computer servers containing advanced GPUs commonly used in artificial intelligence applications.
Prosecutors say the operation relied on a practice known as transshipment, in which goods are routed through intermediate countries before reaching their final destination. U.S. authorities have increasingly focused on such arrangements as companies and individuals seek to evade export restrictions on advanced chips, servers and other technologies subject to national-security controls.
The government alleges the servers could not legally be exported directly to China without special licenses from the Commerce Department.
Instead, prosecutors say the equipment was shipped to countries including Malaysia and Singapore, where export restrictions were less stringent. Once there, the servers were allegedly forwarded to buyers in China.
Investigators also accuse Lui and others of providing U.S. manufacturers with false documentation that concealed the equipment's true destination.
One example cited in court filings involves a January 2024 purchase of 27 servers worth roughly $7.6 million, shipped from Los Angeles to Kuala Lumpur. Prosecutors say a co-conspirator later acknowledged that the servers had been forwarded to a China-based buyer.
The government alleges the broader operation moved more than $300 million worth of restricted technology.
The charges come as the United States continues tightening restrictions on advanced computer chips and AI-related hardware destined for China.
Washington has argued that the most sophisticated semiconductors and computing systems can be used for military, intelligence, and surveillance purposes, making them a national-security concern.
According to prosecutors, the servers involved in the case contained GPUs commonly used in advanced artificial intelligence systems, which the Trump administration now refers to as "Super Intelligence."
Assistant Attorney General John Eisenberg described AI chips as one of the country's most strategically important technologies.
Federal officials allege Lui knowingly circumvented export rules designed to prevent advanced American technology from reaching prohibited users.
The FBI, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service are investigating.
Lui has been charged but not convicted. The allegations are contained in a federal indictment, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
The federal court docket did not identify legal counsel for Lui, according to Bloomberg .

articles.title_orig: David Jackson wins third World 3D title as France triumph in Yankton
articles.title_zh: David Jackson wins third World 3D title as France triumph in Yankton
articles.content_orig:
France‘s David Jackson took a third World 3D title in barebow men after defeating Spain‘s Cesar Vera Bringas in the final at Yankton 2026 World Archery 3D Championships .
The 34-year-old previously won at the championships in 2019 and 2022, the same year he became world field champion.
The barebow women‘s title also went to France, with Virginie Chevrier triumphing at her maiden world championships, defeating reigning European champion Rosemarie Leitner of Austria.
The compound competition was won by Slovenia‘s Tim Jevsnik , defeating multiply decorated field and 3D champion Nico Wiener of Austria. The reigning European champion, France‘s Aude Ama-Cormerais defeated Ingrid Ronacher , another Austrian former champion, for the women‘s title.
Jackson was also part of France‘s four man men‘s team who also took gold at the event yesterday. The wins pushed France to the top of the medal table for the event, ahead of Austria and Russia.
The traditional bow titles went to Denmark‘s Zibrandt Christensen and Germany‘s Judith Wenzl. The latter is the reigning European champion and Christensen takes his second title after a win in 2017.
The individual longbow competition was won by Russia‘s Mikhail Poddevalin and Austria‘s Johanna Pitschmann , the latter one of the older competitors in the field, winning a world title age 63.
Pitschmann’s victory was perhaps less of a surprise to an unsighted bow field notable for the higher average age of the competitors – in a discipline where experience and learned instinct counts for a great deal.

articles.title_orig: Flydubai captain says copilot asked to pray, then struck him from behind; describes exactly how he opened cockpit door
articles.title_zh: Flydubai captain says copilot asked to pray, then struck him from behind; describes exactly how he opened cockpit door
articles.content_orig:
Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel.
The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane.
The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami.
The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives.
In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia".
The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time".
Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it.
Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel.
Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe , the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.
Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar, an Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.
The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.
He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.
In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history.
While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.
It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK.
He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

articles.title_orig: From Global Commitment to National Practice: World Teachers’ Day in Bangladesh
articles.title_zh: From Global Commitment to National Practice: World Teachers’ Day in Bangladesh
articles.content_orig:
Bangladesh marks World Teachers’ Day across the country on 5 October, three years after the Cabinet placed the Day on its annual calendar. The 2026 observance also marks 60 years since the adoption of the ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers. The Recommendation remains a key international reference for teachers’ rights and responsibilities, professional preparation, recruitment, employment and teaching and working conditions. World Teachers’ Day has been observed worldwide since 1994 and is co-convened by UNESCO with the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International.
Bangladesh’s journey towards institutionalizing the Day gained momentum in 2022. On 27 October that year, the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), under the Ministry of Education, coordinated a nationwide Teachers’ Day celebration. DSHE and UNESCO Dhaka Office jointly supported the celebrations and the development of a roadmap to institutionalize the annual observance within government systems. UNESCO subsequently described Bangladesh’s institutionalization of the Day as part of efforts to strengthen recognition of the teaching profession.
This process led to an important policy milestone. In September 2023, the Cabinet decided that Bangladesh would observe World Teachers’ Day every year on 5 October, replacing National Teachers’ Day. The decision placed the global observance within the country’s formal annual calendar and established a basis for regular government-led celebrations.
Since then, the observance has continued to develop as a national platform for recognising teachers. The Government issued a celebration policy in 2024, national recognition was extended to 12 teachers in 2025 and the 2026 arrangements envisage recognition of teachers across the country. This progression from a global observance to a nationally coordinated initiative in 2022 and then to a formal annual government-led observance reflects a shared effort to strengthen the recognition and status of teachers in Bangladesh.
Teachers had marked the Day in Bangladesh before it became an annual national observance. A Ministry of Education description lists World Teachers’ Day among the international days observed by the Bangladesh National Commission for UNESCO. During the reopening of schools in 2021, UNESCO Dhaka and a2i asked teachers to share videos about blended teaching and their wellbeing, as part of activities involving the education ministries and directorates. The call offered Huawei-supplied tablets for the 20 highest-ranked entries.
At the national ceremony on 5 October 2023, seven teachers were honoured . In a message for the occasion, Bangladesh’s then President described World Teachers’ Day as a UNESCO-declared observance . Susan Vize, then Officer in Charge of UNESCO Dhaka, took part as a Guest of Honour and spoke about the need to invest in skilled teachers.
The government issued a celebration policy in 2024 and 12 teachers received national honours in 2025 . The 2026 policy plans recognition for 100 teachers , alongside celebrations beyond the national ceremony.
Iffat Jahan, an assistant teacher at Shah Government Primary School in Rangamati, received a national World Teachers’ Day award in 2025 in primary school category. She said the recognition made her feel more responsible for her teaching and deepened her love for the profession. She also hopes future selections will examine teachers’ work more closely at the local level to identify deserving recipients.
At the 2023 ceremony, Pollob Kumar Voumik, assistant headmaster of Shantipur High School in Khilgaon, said the Day “reminds us of our roles and responsibilities” toward the next generation. Ismot Ara Momotaz, a senior teacher at Government Laboratory High School, spoke of the recognition teachers seek: “Our only expectation is to get proper dignity and honour.”
Those concerns sit at the centre of UNESCO’s 2026 World Teachers’ Day message . It calls on policymakers and society to protect and advance teachers’ status, including their voice in education decisions and the conditions in which they work. Bangladesh’s 2026 celebration policy follows UNESCO’s global theme. Each 5 October is an opportunity to recognise teachers, hear what they need and bring their perspectives into decisions that shape education.

articles.title_orig: For delicate Crepe, it’s a brave new world
articles.title_zh: For delicate Crepe, it’s a brave new world
articles.content_orig:
This is Crepe, a delicate young girl who’s just 1½ years old and weighs only 3 kilograms.
She only recently came to ARK, along with three of her siblings, when her owner moved to a no-pet apartment. And, in the beginning, little Crepe was very good at doing imitations of a rock. She wouldn’t move. She wouldn’t be touched. She’d stay very, very still and refuse to engage in the world around her. Perhaps she thought that if she could just stay still enough, everything would return to what she’d known before.
Now, however, Crepe is beginning to realize that this new world isn’t so bad after all. She is more adventurous and has started to explore her environs, limited as they are. She’ll come out for pats when she notices that the humans bear gifts of food.
Crepe has also discovered toys and how they bring out her joy and her kitten side.
We’d love Crepe to find a new home, preferably along with one of her siblings, which would surely help her quickly gain confidence in her new home.

articles.title_orig: ‘Dabo (Swinney) Should Be Ashamed,’ ‘He Made This Bed’ — CFB World Shows Clemson HC No Mercy As Tigers Get Mauled in Blowout Loss to No. 4 Miami
articles.title_zh: ‘Dabo (Swinney) Should Be Ashamed,’ ‘He Made This Bed’ — CFB World Shows Clemson HC No Mercy As Tigers Get Mauled in Blowout Loss to No. 4 Miami
articles.content_orig:
There was nowhere for Dabo Swinney to hide as his Clemson Tigers were caged by the Miami Hurricanes in what served as a stark reminder of the current state of the program. The unbeaten No. 4 Miami bullied Clemson all the way to a 41-13 rout at Memorial Stadium.
As the Tigers were left to lick their wounds, criticism of Swinney was swift and pointed, with fans and analysts questioning the direction of a program that had been held up as the gold standard in years past.
The Tigers fell to 3-2 after the deflating loss to the high-flying Hurricanes, and social media quickly turned its attention toward Swinney, Clemson's direction, and whether the longtime coach can get the program back among the sport's elite.
After what was the fourth-worst loss for the Tigers under their head coach, fans were quick to ask a pressing question: Is it time for Swinney to step aside?
"Dabo's mad, but not mad enough," wrote one Clemson fan page . "He made this bed with his roster management. Two games against elite rosters, both ending in lopsided losses. Pretty easy to see why. It's about the Jimmy's & the Joe's."
Another Clemson fan account vented its frustrations, writing , "Honestly, Dabo should be ashamed of what this program has become. I'm tired of his 'We've won a lot' BS. This is a huge falloff.
"To go from one of the top programs in the country to a team that is lucky to get more than two TDs per game is a huge disappointment."
Pack Power 247 editor Cory Smith remarked , "This isn't just a change of the guard in the ACC. This is an absolute [expletive]-whooping with no mercy from Mario Cristobal and Miami for Dabo Swinney and the corpse that remains of the program."
PREDICT THE CFB SEASON: PFN's Free CFB Playoff Predictor
One Clemson reporter chimed in , "The fact that Dabo chose this over getting a QB from the portal just shows me that he doesn't give a [expletive]."
Meanwhile, this fan decided to add some perspective, writing , "I understand Clemson might want to move on from Dabo Swinney, but I hope we all remember he made that program nationally relevant.
"Are we really going to say a coach like Dabo, who led Clemson to two national titles, isn't good enough for the program?"
One Miami analyst kept it simple, writing , "Bye bye, Dabo!"
DIVE IN: PFN's Free CFB HQ — Team and Player Stats, Info, and More
The numbers certainly gave Swinney's critics more than enough ammunition to work with. The Tigers managed just 55 rushing yards on 31 attempts tonight, averaging a mere 1.8 yards per carry against Miami's defense.
Clemson quarterback Tait Reynolds, who ranks #161 in the nation with a PFN QB Impact Score of 60.6, threw for 295 yards, but the Tigers never developed enough balance offensively to consistently threaten the Hurricanes.
Clemson entered the matchup ranked #131 in the nation with a PFN Team Offense Impact Score of 61.0 and a Defense Impact Score of 76.3 (#65).
Then there's the case of the self-inflicted mistakes. Clemson committed 10 penalties for 91 yards, including a costly false start near the Miami goal line on third-and-1.
Swinney's reaction to that misstep quickly went viral and served as a fitting image for how the night unfolded.
Miami was also simply far more explosive and ready to go for the jugular. The Hurricanes averaged 6.8 yards per play compared with Clemson's 4.7, finishing with 419 total yards while repeatedly producing chunk plays.

Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.
Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies.
The weapon used has been a key question for investigators, given the stringent security on such a sensitive route. Early reports from passengers on board had suggested it might have been a knife.
The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.
The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. There has been no official confirmation of this.
While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.
Australian authorities confirmed on Sunday they were investigating his "links" to the country, but did not provide any details.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation, citing sources, reported he was issued a student visa in 2014 and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017 before leaving the country.
The ABC said his student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was not enrolled in a course at that time.
Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.
He then completed a three-year distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.
Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!"
The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."
He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".
The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.
He also said investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.
Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.
"I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.
About two and half hours after the plane took off from Dubai International Airport it begun to plunge sharply.
The plane signalled a "general emergency" code, squawk 7700, before switching to squawk 7500, a code reporting "unlawful interference", or hijacking.
In an interview with the BBC, one passenger described the moment he realised that something was wrong.
Almog Itali said: "Suddenly the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down [with] a massive G-force. It was falling down for 20 or 30 seconds, rapidly, and then balanced, and then started once again to fall down."
People then began to rush to the cockpit, he said.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Thursday that the alarm was raised onboard by an Israeli woman, Tali Manes, who heard a commotion coming from the cockpit.
Her husband, Zvika, along with three other men - Yaniv Hayun, Dr Shota Musayev and Asaf Rajuan - entered the cockpit after Capt Machchhar managed to open the door despite his injuries.
Hayun said, in a video released by the prime minister's office, that the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".
Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.
He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there," he said.
In an interview with CNN on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu said the stabbed pilot, passengers and second crew had "managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster".

articles.title_orig: Health Policy Watch | COVID-19 drops out of world’s top 10 causes of death for first time since pandemic began
articles.title_zh: Health Policy Watch | COVID-19 drops out of world’s top 10 causes of death for first time since pandemic began
articles.content_orig:
COVID-19 dropped out of the world’s 10 leading causes of death in 2023 for the first time since the pandemic began in 2020, and only two years after it topped the list, according to new World Health Organization estimates released Friday (2 October).
The virus directly killed an estimated 0.9 million people in 2023, ranking 14th, as global life expectancy climbed back to near its pre-pandemic level. WHO declared an end to COVID-19 as a global health emergency in May that year.
Revised figures now rank COVID-19 as the world’s leading cause of death in 2021, with 9.4 million direct deaths. WHO’s earlier estimates had placed it second that year. Together with 5.3 million deaths in 2020, the new figures put the virus’s direct toll in the first two years of the pandemic at 14.7 million.

articles.title_orig: Bernie Sanders makes a late push for California billionaire tax
articles.title_zh: Bernie Sanders makes a late push for California billionaire tax
articles.content_orig:
Google cofounder Sergey Brin has now spent more than nine figures combating California’s proposed wealth tax.
According to filings , Brin donated a total of $102 million to the group Building a Better California, a PAC and political advocacy organization opposing the state’s billionaire tax and supporting other pro-business policies and housing and infrastructure affordability. Campaign filings show efforts to block this tax have exceeding $187 million, making Brin the largest sole contributor to the effort. Contributions supporting the bill have meanwhile reached about $32 million.
Proposition 40 , which will be on the ballot in November, would impose a one-time, 5% tax on California’s 200 billionaires, with 90% of the revenue from the proposed measure going toward the state’s health care program and 10% going toward education, food assistance, and administration. Brin, with a net worth of nearly $260 billion , could owe about $13 billion as a result of the tax.
California, the most populous state, has become the epicenter of the conversation around the K-shaped economy, or the diverging fortunes of those with wealth and those without it. While the Golden State has a $4 trillion GDP, making its economy about the same size as the United Kingdom’s, it also has 18% of its residents living below the poverty line , the highest in the country, in part because of its high cost of living.
The ballot measure has caused an uproar among some of California’s wealthiest individuals such as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and PayPal cofounder Peter Thiel, both of whom have donated to organizations against the measure. Brin compared the proposal to his socialist Soviet upbringing.
“I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same place,” he told the New York Times in a statement in April.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has joined these tech billionaires in combating the measure, arguing the tax would hurt the state by eroding its tax base, ultimately reducing key revenue for social services.
“The fact is it actually will reduce investments in education,” Newsom said in a Bloomberg Businessweek interview earlier this year. “It will reduce investments in teachers and librarians, childcare. It will reduce investments in firefighting and police.”
The opposition to Prop 40 may, in some ways, be a self-fulfilling prophecy, as billionaires including Brin shift business entities out of California in favor of states without similar wealth taxes. Brin now lists Nevada as his residence, according to state records. Larry Page, who cofounded Google alongside Brin, has converted several of his assets out of California, including Koop, his family office, which was incorporated in Delaware in December 2025. Oceankind, an ocean science nonprofit founded by Page’s wife, Lucy Southworth, in 2018 , was similarly incorporated in Delaware around the same time. Brin, for his own part, reportedly bought a $51 million home near Miami Beach in March.
There’s not yet clear evidence to indicate these billionaires’ anxieties about the future of California are well-founded. On one hand, the six billionaires expected to leave California—Brin, Page, Thiel, as well as car loan magnate Don Hankey, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, and director Steven Spielberg—would have collectively generated about $27 billion in tax revenue, about one-fourth of the $100 billion the proposal is expected to raise through taxes over five years.
On the other hand, billionaires were already paying so little in California income tax their departure may not pack as much of a punch as anticipated. A working paper published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in May noted billionaires residing in the state paid $4.1 billion in income tax last year, about 0.2% of their collective $2 trillion net worth, meaning that even if every billionaire were to leave the state, it would take about 25 years for lost income tax revenue to cancel out the $100 billion sum California is projected to get from the tax. Even if a billionaire mass exodus included one-quarter of the state’s wealthiest residents, it would take a century to equal the $100 billion windfall.
“The proposed one-off California billionaire tax of 5%, payable over five years, is both small relative to California billionaires’ wealth gains and large relative to the taxes they currently pay,” the authors wrote.
A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Aug. 11, 2026.

articles.content_orig:
The US president urges people to call the Arkansas Republican, who opposes making daylight saving time permanent
US President Donald Trump shared online the supposed phone number of a Republican US senator on Saturday in an escalating dispute over making daylight saving time permanent.
In a social media post, the president urged people to call a phone number he said belonged to Senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican who opposes the Trump-backed Sunshine Protection Act. The act would end the twice-yearly practice ‌of changing clocks by one hour.
Trump says most Americans want more afternoon sunlight, but Cotton has argued the change would plunge early risers into darkness in winter.
“Everybody in Arkansas, Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill,” Trump said on social media.

articles.title_orig: Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if US turns them away
articles.title_zh: Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if US turns them away
articles.content_orig:
President Trump defended the rapid buildout of massive data centers Saturday as he rallied supporters in Ohio to turn out for Republican candidates in next month’s midterm elections — warning that blocking the tech projects would hand an advantage to China.
“There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump told supporters at the campaign rally outside Dayton — where he urged voters to back Republican Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.
Trump repeatedly told the crowd in the battleground state to act as though he himself were on the ballot in the November 3 midterms.
“Please pretend that I’m on the ballot, and you need to turn out for a midterm victory,” he said.
Trump said his administration was taking “historic action” to make sure large technology companies behind data centers benefit surrounding communities.
The president tied the data center boom to the global race over artificial intelligence, saying the US was ahead of China in what he repeatedly called “superintelligence.”
Trump said China “doesn’t want to see us,” adding, “We’re beating China” in the technology race as he argued against turning data centers away from the US.
At the same time, Trump backed legislation pushed by Husted that he said would “stop data centers from raising electricity costs and require them to pay their own way.”
Trump said nearly every Senate Democrat had voted days earlier to block the measure.
He vowed to sign the Ratepayer Protection Act “into law immediately within 24 hours” if Republicans prevailed.
The surge in data center development has triggered a bipartisan backlash across the country as communities grapple with the enormous amounts of electricity, water and land required to power the facilities.
The biggest fight has centered on who should pay for the infrastructure needed to serve the projects.
Utilities may need to build new power plants, substations and transmission lines for massive data center loads, raising concerns that households and other businesses could be stuck with higher bills if those costs are spread across the broader rate base.
Water use, noise and sprawling footprints have also fueled resistance, particularly in areas where projects sit near homes or rely on strained water supplies.
Critics have also questioned generous state and local tax breaks for facilities that can cost billions of dollars to build but employ relatively few workers once construction is finished.
The political pressure has prompted officials in several states to rethink the incentives and fast-track approvals once used to lure the industry.
Some states have paused tax breaks or permitting, while others have pushed special utility rates and requirements aimed at making developers shoulder more of the cost of serving their facilities.
Trump was in Ohio after stops in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week as part of what he says will be a 32-day jaunt ahead of the midterms.

articles.title_orig: Young Chinese hire ‘life stand-ins’ to cook and care for elderly parents amid booming trend
articles.title_zh: Young Chinese hire ‘life stand-ins’ to cook and care for elderly parents amid booming trend
articles.content_orig:
Outsourcing life’s mundane tasks buys us freedom, but risks relinquishing the experience of living, says online observer
From cooking and attending hospital visits to doing the actual quarrelling, paid “life stand-ins” are stepping in to manage these tasks, along with errands and awkward moments that many young Chinese would rather avoid.
This trend, known as the “stand-in economy,” is gaining traction among time-strapped consumers who are willing to pay for convenience when daily responsibilities exceed their time, patience, or expertise.
First widely reported by mainland media in 2024, the movement has since blossomed into a vast market for highly personalised errand services.
On RedNote, posts about paid handicraft and assembly assistance have garnered over 120 million views. For example, some users buy intricate Lego sets but lack the time needed to assemble them, opting instead to hire professional builders.

articles.title_orig: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
articles.title_zh: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
articles.content_orig:
‘The Big Weekend Show’ panel discusses protests in France over complaints about teacher shortages, school days and deteriorating facilities.
France’s violent student protests are fueling fresh warnings about the consequences of open-border immigration policies, with the unrest being held up as a "cautionary tale" for the U.S.
"I would also say as we’re sitting here in beautiful New York City, this is a cautionary tale," "The Big Weekend Show" co-host Tomi Lahren said Saturday.
She continued: "This is something we’re learning from Europe, and we would be wise to learn from Europe. They decided they wanted to have open borders. They decided they wanted diversity as their strength, and of course, Joe Biden tried that for four years. We’re undoing that currently."
FRANCE'S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT
Policemen stand in front of burning garbage as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools in Paris on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
Lahren posited that "when you let so many people come into your country, leech off of your system, then the people who are from there are going to at some point get upset."
She said that anger often becomes misplaced and, "they end up lighting things on fire, which I think is stupid no matter what you’re angry with, but it’s no doubt these countries that say we’re going to be a global home for everybody, they end up paying the price, and it’s usually the native Frenchmen, or whenever they are that end up paying the highest price."
Students in Paris began to protest late last month against what they deemed as overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, long school days and deteriorating conditions, blaming the government for not investing enough in education.
REPUBLICAN GLEE ERUPTS AS WHITE HOUSE BOASTS SHARP DECLINE IN IMMIGRATION FROM MUSLIM-MAJORITY NATIONS
A student kicks a tear gas canister during a protest against under-resourced schools in Paris on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
The demonstrations started peacefully in Paris’ poorer suburbs but quickly spread to Paris itself, then went nationwide in cities like Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours, Nantes, Toulouse ​and Lille, becoming increasingly violent as they expanded.
The protests were also fueled by the government’s 2027 budget unveiling on Thursday, which showed education spending would rise by only 1.7%, excluding teacher pensions, an increase which is below the rate of inflation, Reuters reported.
Rioters have committed arson, vandalism, thrown objects at police and even assaulted people in some cases, prompting authorities to respond with tear gas and rubber bullets.
TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS
Students block the entrance of Voltaire high school in Paris as they protest against under-resourced schools on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
More than 5,000 protesters were arrested this week across the country, according to Reuters, and more than 400 schools remained closed as of Friday.
Euronews reported Friday that at least 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, have been injured since the unrest began, along with roughly 170 students.
More than 100 high schools have suffered what Education Minister Édouard Geffray described as "severe damage."
French intelligence agencies told a government crisis meeting Thursday that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard-left France Unbowed Party, known as LFI, Reuters reported Friday.
LIZ PEEK: ANGRY, AFFLUENT AND ADRIFT — WHAT'S DRIVING SOME YOUNG AMERICANS TO VIOLENCE
Anti-riot police officers face protesting students carrying out blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris on Friday. (Lou Benoist / AFP via Getty Images)
LFI has denied the allegations and accused President Emmanuel Macron 's government of politicizing the protests ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.
Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the unrest began with legitimate concerns but has since evolved into something far more serious.

"The students’ grievances about missing teachers and deteriorating schools were real at first," Rodan-Benzaquen said. "But dousing a principal in gasoline and attacking firefighters are acts of extreme violence. What makes this politically significant is the effort to turn frustration over schools into a much broader confrontation with the government."
Fox News' Efrat Lachter contributed to this report.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Cornell president says university 'must do better' on handling of sexual assault allegations
articles.title_zh: Cornell president says university 'must do better' on handling of sexual assault allegations
articles.content_orig:
Cornell University President Michael I. Kotlikoff said Saturday his school's administration "must do better" amid the criticism and fallout of its investigation into allegations made by a former student that she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024.
"I believe we as an administration and we as a community must do better," Kotlikoff said in a video message posted online Saturday. "We must do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe and everyone before her and anyone after her from ever happening again."
The former student, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit last month against the university and seven men, alleging she was drugged and raped in October 2024 at the university's Chi Phi fraternity chapter when she was 20 years old.
"This has been one of the most difficult weeks in our history, and I know many of you are angry, saddened and struggling," Kotlikoff said.
Back in 2024, the Tompkins County district attorney found that "there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges." No criminal charges have been filed in the case.
However, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said this week that he was never given the full transcript of Jane Doe's two-day interview with campus police that occurred in November 2024, about three weeks after the incident, but was only presented a six-page sworn statement based on that interview.
Cornell University initially said its police department provided the results of the school's Title IX investigation to the DA. However, in an FAQ published on its website regarding the allegations, the university said in an Oct. 1 update that it "shared the victim's sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."
The Snapchat screenshot refers to a Snapchat group chat that involved members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of the alleged rape.
Van Houten said this week he is reopening the investigation, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who has been publicly critical of Van Houten's approach to the case, said she had appointed State Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to lead the investigation.
Kotlikoff revealed that the school would be hiring an outside law firm to conduct an "independent review" of "all aspects of Cornell's handling of the 2024 matter." The school has said that it supports the state's criminal probe, which Kotlikoff reiterated Saturday.
The school president admitted the situation "raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported."
Kotlikoff earlier this week disclosed that the school's Title IX investigation resulted in two of the accused being expelled and two being suspended for at least two semesters. One had already graduated before any punishment could be handed down, Kotlikoff  said, and two were found not to be responsible for sexual misconduct.
"I also hear the frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough about what the university did after the assault was reported, which has led to distrust," Kotlikoff said in his video. "There are real legal and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make greater effort to explain what we can, to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken, and to be more transparent."
He noted that in 2025, in the wake of the initial investigation into Jane Doe's allegations, the university established the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault and endorsed the task force's recommendations.
Kotlikoff said in the coming weeks, the university will create opportunities for community members, including parents of current students, to question and talk to school leadership.
"This is a defining moment in Cornell's history," Kotlikoff said. "We must lead the way. We owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe."

articles.title_orig: Cornell University police made drug arrest hours before alleged sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell University police made drug arrest hours before alleged sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
Cornell University police made a drug-related arrest at a fraternity house 22 hours before a former student alleges she was drugged and sexually assaulted there, according to police records.
The Cornell Daily Sun reported Saturday that campus police responded to the Chi Phi fraternity house shortly after 1 a.m. on Oct. 19, 2024, made a drug-related arrest and referred an individual to the university’s Office of Student Conduct.
The archived police log cited by the Sun and reviewed by NBC News does not identify the individual or the drugs involved or establish a connection between the drug incident and the alleged assault later that night.
Cornell University had no comment. Its police department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The former Cornell student, identified as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit last month against the university and seven Chi Phi brothers, alleging she was sexually assaulted over the course of hours that night while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana.
In a police interview conducted after the alleged assault and documented in records obtained by NBC News, a woman told investigators she had seen a fraternity member with a bag of ketamine about two months earlier. She also said he had previously overdosed and been transported for treatment. The interview does not establish when that occurred or whether she witnessed it.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said in a video message Saturday afternoon that what Jane Doe alleges is “deeply disturbing” and raised questions about the investigation that followed.
“I believe we as an administration, and we as a community, must do better,” he said.
NBC News reported Friday that Cornell police interviewed witnesses and received anonymous tips in the first weeks of their investigation, but Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten did not review that additional information before deciding not to bring charges.
Van Houten said he based his decision on Jane Doe’s initial six-page statement to police, which he argued did not allege criminality. Her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, has said authorities failed to conduct a thorough investigation and prejudged the events based on her statement that she had consented to parts of the night.
Gov. Kathy Hochul on Thursday appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to consider whether criminal charges are appropriate.
“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript” of her interview, Hochul asked at a news conference Friday.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.
Shayna Jacobs is a national reporter for NBC News digital.
